entries.title: Federal Immigration Agents Shoot and Wound a Man in New York
entries.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he called President Trump about the incident and hopes to end ICE enforcement actions in the city.
entries.content:
A federal immigration agent shot a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon, city officials said.

The shooting occurred around 4 p.m. in Marble Hill, a Manhattan neighborhood that borders the Bronx, the New York Police Department said in a post on X. The person was conscious and is being treated at a hospital. No NYPD officers were involved or at the scene at the time of the shooting, the department said.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the man and a 5-year-old had been surrounded by agents, though the child was physically unharmed after the altercation. The mayor called the event “unconscionable” and said he had called President Donald Trump about the “incredibly serious situation.”

“I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city,” Mamdani wrote in a post on X.

He ended the post by calling to “abolish ICE.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul wrote in a post on X that she expected federal officials to “provide a full and transparent accounting” of the shooting.

When reached for comment, the NYPD referred The Washington Sun to its earlier post on X. The mayor’s office, the Department of Homeland Security and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This is a developing story.

entries.title: Jon Ossoff Accuses Mike Collins of Having ‘Hired Half the Third Reich’
entries.summary: The Democratic senator made his opponent’s staff and family members, who have propagated white supremacist views, a focus of the Georgia Senate debate.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff hammered Rep. Mike Collins, his opponent in the Georgia Senate race, over his connections to staff and family members who have propagated white supremacist views.

He called Collins a “bigot” and at one point in the hour-long debate on Thursday said he had “hired half the Third Reich to staff [his] congressional office.”

“Imagine running for the U.S. Senate while neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your home. That’s Mike Collins,” Ossoff said, referring to Collins’ son-in-law David Alan Scheer II, who reportedly lives on a property owned by Collins.

Collins, who has a history of posting inflammatory posts from his account on X, has been dogged by a string of scandals involving his staff and family members throughout the race, including several who have far-right connections.

Collins fired a chief of staff over the summer following reports that the staffer had been in a group chat with prominent white nationalists, in which the staffer said he was trying to free an imprisoned Holocaust denier. Another former staffer posted Nazi imagery on his personal X account. And a July CNN investigation into Scheer unearthed a history of promoting far-right conspiracy theories online.

Collins has previously issued statements condemning his staffers’ comments but has dodged questions about his son-in-law. When asked by moderators on Thursday to address the issue, Collins suggested that he had spoken with his son-in-law about it.

“I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is, and I tell him that too,” Collins said, without specifying who he was referring to. “It’s wrong.”

Collins also noted he has fired staffers over their online comments.

Ossoff, who has consistently led in polling and has a massive cash advantage to Collins, repeatedly steered the debate back to those controversies.

Collins blamed the “craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing” for an alleged death threat he received, which resulted in the arrest of a man in Buffalo, New York, last week. The suspect was accused of sending death threats to Collins and his son-in-law via Instagram.

In a copy of the arrest warrant obtained by The Washington Sun, deputies alleged the suspect sent a message saying, “Ill come to Jackson and smoke you cracka ass and ya father-in-law.”

National Republican groups in recent weeks have shifted resources away from swing states like North Carolina to defend turf in increasingly competitive red states, such as Kansas and South Carolina, The Sun previously reported.

Collins’ struggles against Ossoff may be precipitating a similar retreat in Georgia. Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund has canceled nearly $2 million in Georgia ad buys, The Sun reported Thursday.

entries.title: The First Debate in Michigan’s Heated Senate Race Was ... Intense
entries.summary: Republican nominee Mike Rogers suggested Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed may have family on a terrorist watch list.
entries.content:
The Michigan Senate debate on Thursday was as heated and personal as the rest of the race has been.

Republican nominee Mike Rogers repeatedly called Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed a “glitchy AI chatbot” and suggested the Muslim American has ties to terrorists. El-Sayed called Rogers cowardly and accused him of going after the “Peeping Tom vote” by supporting local government control of Flock cameras.

The moderator, Rick Albin of WOOD TV8, said after an ad break that the intensity wasn’t limited to on-air time: “In the 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue into commercial.”

The Michigan race is one of the most competitive in the country, with the open seat rated as a “toss up” by The Cook Political Report. Winning the seat could be the difference between controlling the U.S. Senate for both Democrats and Republicans.

Each candidate was eager to talk about affordability, which has been a focus for most congressional races across the country. El-Sayed was quick to attach President Donald Trump’s economic track record to Rogers’ “direct line” to the White House, reminding the audience that Rogers has been in Congress before.

“He’s going to make this about him and me,” El-Sayed said, predicting the rest of the debate's tone. “But really, it’s about you and whether you can afford your gas and your groceries.”

Rogers began to address the affordability-concerns question with an answer about a diesel rebate but got off track when he prodded at the legitimacy of El-Sayed’s medical license. El-Sayed received his medical degree from Columbia University and has a doctorate in public health from Oxford University, but Republicans have seized on him having little history of treating patients. El-Sayed is not licensed to practice medicine in Michigan.

“If somebody came into his office and he tried to treat that patient, he’d go to jail,” Rogers said.

El-Sayed threw his fair share of punches, asking Rogers to “just be serious, my guy,” in response to his opponent’s economic policy. Later on, El-Sayed called Rogers “my guy” again; Rogers shot back by calling El-Sayed “brother.”

Artificial intelligence and data centers have been hot topics throughout the Michigan race, with both candidates calling for some level of regulation on the technology. El-Sayed is running on public ownership of AI companies and regulation of Flock surveillance technology by the federal government. Rogers has advocated for a temporary moratorium on data centers and supports letting local governments control Flock cameras, but he said he doesn’t approve of them being misused.

El-Sayed launched an anti-Flock ad blitz earlier this week, which included a website with blown-up photos of Rogers’ face with “Mike Rogers is watching you” underneath.

The quips grew more personal when Rogers said Flock cameras could be used to catch terrorists.

“Why would that bother you?” Rogers said. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the watch list …”

El-Sayed jumped in and dared his opponent to finish his sentence.

“Go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing around it.”

Rogers then brought up El-Sayed’s birth mother, who’s been accused of working for a group designated as a terrorist organization. At another point in the debate, Rogers suggested El-Sayed has relationships to groups like Hamas, Hezbollah and Al-Qaeda. These allegations have been reported to be misleading by the Detroit Free Press, and El-Sayed’s campaign has not yet commented on the allegation about his biological mother.

In Rogers’ closing pitch, he warned that El-Sayed was not the right choice to represent Michigan, only mentioning himself in his final seconds.

“We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.

El-Sayed similarly focused on Rogers in his final 30 seconds, although he tried to circle back to his starting message about focusing on Michiganders.

“I told you what this debate was going to be: him pointing at me and saying all kinds of foreign names, or him talking about himself,” El-Sayed said.

A post-debate camera angle showed Rogers leaning over to El-Sayed for a quick handshake before disappearing offstage. The candidates are expected to be back on the debate stage Oct. 21 in Detroit.

entries.title: House Republican Campaign Chief Launches Defensive Spending in His Own Race
entries.summary: The ad reservations made by North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson suggest he’s being cautious about his own reelection.
entries.content:
Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has reserved tens of thousands of dollars in TV ad buys in his North Carolina district as Republicans fight to hold onto their slim majority.

The ad buys are striking because Hudson, tasked with protecting the Republican House majority, represents a district that President Donald Trump won by more than 15 percentage points in 2024. The rocky political climate for Republicans has members in solid red seats taking very few chances ahead of the midterm elections.

A source with access to an ad tracking database told The Washington Sun that Hudson’s campaign had reserved north of $200,000 in spending. Federal Communications Commission records verified a flurry of activity by Hudson’s campaign in the tens of thousands of dollars this week.

Hudson’s campaign did not dispute the $200,000 figure.

“Congressman Hudson runs hard every cycle, and this one is no different. He was on air at home in 2022, he was on air in 2024, and he's on air now. He earns every vote, every time,” said Cam Mills, Hudson’s campaign manager, in a statement.

His team did not provide documentation suggesting past cycle spending was comparable to the spending his campaign is doing now.

In one 30-second spot, Hudson, sitting at a bar counter, speaks against stock trading by members of Congress and name-checks former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi.

A Democratic-leaning pollster surveyed the race last month and found Hudson leading Democrat Richard Ojeda, 46% to 42%.

“I think this may be a recognition that some Republicans who would have felt comfortable not having to advertise, not having to do massive campaigning are probably seeing some writing on the wall of Democratic enthusiasm,” Michael Bitzer, professor of politics at Catawba College, told The Sun of the spending. “This may be an attempt just to shore up their walls around their district.”

Hudson, who as chair of the NRCC spends a lot of time traveling and fundraising, hasn’t faced a competitive challenger since 2020, when Patricia Timmons-Goodson came within 6 percentage points. Odeja previously served in the West Virginia state Senate.

“RICHARD HUDSON IS ON TV. WE NEED TO BE TOO,” Ojeda’s campaign posted on Facebook on Thursday in a fundraising plea.

Ojeda’s campaign reported raising $2.2 million compared to Hudson’s $3.2 million as of the end of June.

The “ad buy does not mean that the ship's going down, but it does mean that they're having to pay attention to it,” Chris Cooper, professor of political science at Western Carolina University told The Sun.

Hudson’s ad spend also reflects broader Republican anxiety over North Carolina.

This summer, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee moved Hudson’s district to its “districts in play” list, though The Cook Political Report still categorizes the district as solid Republican.

North Carolina is also the setting of a competitive Senate race between Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley, which is drawing national attention and could have implications for the House races in the state.

“If Republicans are less likely to show up because they're not fired up about Whatley, then that's going to hurt Republicans downballot,” Cooper said.

A recent AARP poll shows Cooper leading Whatley by 11 percentage points.

Last week, the Republican Senate Leadership Fund pulled out of the state in favor of spending in Kansas and South Carolina. The Raleigh News & Observer reported Wednesday that Whatley had paused his ads in order to rethink strategy.

entries.title: D.C. Schools May Soon Have a Big Problem: Fewer Kids
entries.summary: Birth rates are down and enrollment is flat, meaning tough questions could lie ahead.
entries.content:
Earlier this week, each and every one of D.C.’s public and charter schools did something relatively unspectacular: They counted their kids.

Routine as it may be, the annual count is critical, helping D.C. officials determine exactly how many kids are enrolled citywide. And since funding is attached to enrollment, the count is how D.C. calculates how much money each school will get for the year.

This year, though, the count may count for more.

Relatively flat enrollment in D.C.’s public and charter schools last year is raising concerns that the city may soon face the same downward trend that other states, counties and cities have started experiencing, largely because of declining birth rates but also decreases in the number of families coming into the system or choosing to stay.

While officials and experts say there’s no immediate crisis, they add that a possible decline in enrollment — after almost 15 years of steady increases — would prompt difficult and uncomfortable questions and policy choices. That could include potentially closing schools, a route Maryland’s Montgomery County is considering.

“We are in a situation where we should be looking at these trends, because we don’t want to get to a point where we're at a low and don’t have policies to address it,” said Anoosha Imran, an education research analyst with the D.C. Policy Center, a local think tank.

Minus a brief dip during the pandemic, enrollment in D.C. schools has steadily increased over the last two decades, jumping from some 71,280 students in DCPS and charter schools in the 2008-09 school year to 99,555 students in 2024-25.

That largely tracks with the years that D.C.’s economy and population boomed, as did births. Those peaked in 2016, when 9,854 D.C.-resident children were born. But it’s been a steady decline since then, and in 2025 only 7,318 such births were recorded in the city.

“We watch that number particularly carefully, and birth rates become a very important part of our long-term projections because they go through the system,” said Paul Kihn, D.C.’s deputy mayor for education.

The lower birth rates are playing out most clearly in the earlier grades in D.C. schools, notably in the number of families enrolling their kids in pre-K for 3- and 4-year-olds, which has been free in D.C. since 2009. According to data from Kihn’s office, enrollment in pre-K dropped 3 percent from the 2024-25 school year to 2025-26. And there are hints it might continue: The number of applications for schools through D.C.’s universal lottery tool hit 20,987 this year, down from 23,312 two years ago.

In the past, people moving into D.C. could offset the decreases in local births, but that has recently changed — in large part because of federal immigration policies. And those same policies may have contributed to one of the biggest enrollment decreases D.C. schools saw in the 2025-26 school year: Latino students, whose enrollment fell 3.8%.

Kihn said it’s too early to panic; he hopes if any enrollment declines occur this school year, they are gentle. “But if it's something bigger than that, then that would be concerning,” he said.

If the enrollment decline picks up steam, city officials and experts agree it could prompt difficult decisions about whether to keep certain schools open — especially as the city’s budget is getting leaner. Those conversations would likely initially focus on schools that are already underenrolled. According to an annual assessment of school utilization across D.C., 18 DCPS schools and 15 charter schools are under 50% enrolled relative to their capacity.

“It’s hard to operate schools that are significantly underenrolled. It can be harmful for the rest of the District. It’s also bad for those students. How do you provide those students with robust services if you only have 200 to 300 students? It’s very expensive to have a nurse, it’s very expensive in high school to have a range of AP courses,” said Chad Aldeman, an educational analyst and consultant, speaking this week during a conference organized by the D.C. Policy Center.

But closing underenrolled schools would pose challenges. Many are in Wards 7 and 8, where incomes and educational indicators have lagged other parts of D.C. Additionally, past rounds of school closures — 23 in 2008 and 13 in 2013 — targeted a number of DCPS schools in those neighborhoods.

Responding to Aldeman, Kaya Henderson, who was DCPS chancellor from 2010 to 2016 and oversaw one round of school closures, argued that any future decisions on closing schools have to be based on more than just raw enrollment numbers.

“I want to resist the frame that let’s just look at places that are underenrolled and cut there, because over in Wards 7 and 8 those kids need a more robust educational infrastructure than potentially kids in Ward 3. That’s just our reality,” she said.

Kihn said that as decisions like these approach, DCPS and charters — which operate independently from each other — will have to cooperate and coordinate, something that historically hasn’t happened between two sectors that were set up to compete.

“What you don't want is if you lose thousands of kids, for example, and then you've got DCPS over here making some decisions about how they should respond and you've got the charter sector over here making some decisions,” he said. “What you want to have is a coherent citywide approach.”

Officials and experts say that D.C. shouldn’t just assume the inevitability of school enrollment dropping and the difficult responses that would require, but also find ways to encourage families to remain in the city. That includes continuing to invest in the city’s schools, which have seen gains in test scores and achievement, while also taking steps to make D.C. more affordable for families.

“When you look at things like how expensive it is to raise a child in the District when your average cost of early learning is $26,000 a year on top of some of the most expensive rent in the country, it is hard to have and grow a family in the District,” said Joanna Blotner, government affairs director for D.C. Action, which advocates for kid-friendly policies. “All of those things need to be taken into consideration.”

Blotner said D.C. should continue pushing to expand the supply of child care and bring down its cost, something that Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George, who is likely to be the city’s next mayor, has said she will focus on.

“If we have folks who are investing in enrolling their kids in early-learning programs and seeing the District as family-friendly,” Blotner said, “they’re more likely to want to stay in the District long-term.”

entries.title: Major Unions and Business Groups Clash Over Defense Contractor Stock Buybacks
entries.summary: The fight pits organized labor against corporate America as Congress and the president push defense firms to prioritize arms production.
entries.content:
The United Auto Workers, Teamsters, United Steelworkers and four other major unions are urging Congress to restrict stock buybacks and dividends by defense contractors, wading into a fight over how weapons makers spend billions of dollars in taxpayer revenue.

The unions are backing a provision in the Senate’s defense policy bill that is opposed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other major business groups, pitting organized labor against corporate America over efforts in Congress and the Trump administration to push weapons companies to invest more in arms production. Business groups warn the move would set a precedent for federal overreach into private industry

The fight has scrambled traditional political alliances. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) and Mike Lee (R-Utah) championed the Senate provision, while President Donald Trump has also targeted defense contractor stock buybacks, dividends and executive compensation. In a January executive order, Trump directed the Pentagon to restrict those payments at contractors deemed to be underperforming or making weapons too slowly.

The provision would bar the Pentagon from awarding contracts to companies that repurchase shares, pay dividends or make other capital distributions, unless the defense secretary grants a waiver tied to a qualifying defense investment plan.

In a letter sent this week to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees, the unions urged lawmakers to preserve Section 815 of the Senate’s 2027 National Defense Authorization Act as the chambers negotiate a final version of the bill. The unions say they represent millions of workers, including those at major defense contractors and their suppliers.

The unions argue the industry is shortchanging workers on pay while rewarding shareholders with billions in stock buybacks and dividends.

“The working class makes the defense industry run, but instead of investing in our national and economic security, companies like Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Woodward, and dozens more spend taxpayer dollars on Wall Street payoffs to enrich the billionaires,” UAW President Shawn Fain said in a statement.

The unions pointed to Trump’s actions as evidence Congress should go further.

Warren, Hawley and Lee have said the five largest defense contractors have spent more than $100 billion on stock buybacks and dividends since 2020 — more than twice what they spent on capital expenditures. The unions said spending on buybacks and dividends by major defense contractors fell 36% after Trump’s executive order, which they say shows the restrictions are workable.

The unions said labor disputes and work stoppages over the past two years at Boeing, Lockheed, General Dynamics, Textron, GE Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney show that the industry’s spending priorities are leaving its workforce behind.

The U.S. Chamber and more than 40 other business and industry groups previously urged lawmakers to strip Section 815 from the Senate bill, warning that the restrictions would discourage companies from doing business with the Pentagon just as the government is trying to attract new suppliers and private investment into the defense industry.

In a July letter to Senate Armed Services Committee leaders, the groups argued that stock buybacks and dividends benefit millions of Americans who hold shares directly or through retirement accounts. They also warned that the restrictions could hurt employees whose stock ownership plans rely on dividend payments, and they disputed the idea that companies are sacrificing investment in production to reward shareholders.

The business groups also warned that the restrictions would give Washington unprecedented influence over corporate financial decisions, setting a precedent that could extend well beyond the defense industry.

“By prohibiting dividends, share repurchases, and other capital distributions absent a government waiver, Section 815 would shift responsibility for ordinary capital allocation decisions from corporate leadership to Washington,” the groups wrote.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Subtracting Students
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 9, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Declining student enrollment, Metro fare evasion and the Commanders’ rough start. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. Bright skies despite some high clouds, light breezes, low humidity and highs in the mid-70s. October, you’re doing great. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

Kids, what’s 99,555 minus 99,329? 

The answer is 226, and that’s the number of students that D.C. schools lost over the last two school years.

That decline in school enrollment may not seem like much, but city officials and experts tell The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle that it may be the start of a downward trend that could prompt some difficult questions and policy decisions in D.C.’s public and charter schools.

Some of the concerns over future school enrollment stem from births in D.C., which have been dropping steadily over the last decade. While in 2016 there were 9,854 D.C.-resident children born, last year that number stood at 7,318 — a 25% decrease.

“We watch that number particularly carefully, and birth rates become a very important part of our long-term projections because they go through the system,” says Paul Kihn, D.C.’s deputy mayor for education.

Other factors are also at play. The number of people moving into D.C. has slowed, especially among the international set — and federal immigration policies are partly to blame. Those same policies have also led to an even larger drop in school enrollment among Latino students.

There’s no crisis yet, but experts say D.C. officials need to start talking about options now. As enrollment drops, they may have to consider closing some schools. But which ones? And with two separate school systems in D.C. — traditional public schools and independent public charter schools — coordination and cooperation will be critical.

Advocates also say D.C. needs to redouble efforts to make the city more affordable, especially reducing the cost of child care. “If we have folks who are investing in enrolling their kids in early learning programs and seeing the District as family friendly,” says Joanna Blotner of D.C. Action, “they’re more likely to want to stay in the District long term.”

That’s just simple math, right?





DEEP DIVE

Metro Fare Gates (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)
Metro officials are considering a new solution to fare evasion: Expanding the power to issue citations to Metro Special Police Department officers, Metro employees, or, even, civilians. The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports that the idea was discussed during the agency’s Finance and Capital Committee meeting Thursday.

The concept is still a work in progress, Metro General Manager Randy Clarke told The Sun. But the system would love to grant “either civilians or special police” the ability to issue fare evasion citations.

Though the Metro Transit Police issued 11,000 citations during the first six months of the year, only 1,853 resulted in payments and court appearances, according to Metro data. Though fare evasion citations have increased in recent years, most evasion cases are thrown out, The Sun reported in June.

The proposal was just one in a slate of “fare concepts” that are going to be discussed during the 2028 budget cycle. Other ideas include expanding D.C.’s Kids Ride Free program to include Maryland and Virginia, introducing a utilization-based park and ride pricing structure and, notably, increasing fares.

Under the proposed concepts, Metrobus and Metrorail fares would increase by 11.1%. Beginning in July 2027, fares would range from $2.50 to $7.50. Tom Webster, Metro’s chief officer for strategy and planning, said the agency recognizes “that any fare increase is difficult for customers.” Fares last rose by 12.5% in 2024.

Since fares pay for service, the increase may be necessary to “offset the inflationary cost increases that Metro has seen,” Webster said. The energy, fuel and labor costs have increased as inflation has remained high, Clarke told reporters after the meeting: “We would love to not be in a position to raise fares, but that is part of our cost challenge.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

RFK is MIA. A bronze bust of Robert F. Kennedy has gone missing from the lawn outside his namesake stadium, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. It was “removed by an unknown manner” and reported stolen on Oct. 1.

There are still many unknowns about the Purple Line, the light-rail train that will connect Bethesda to New Carrollton, including its opening date. But we know how payment will work: SmartTrip cards, the CharmPass mobile app, cash or credit. The tickets will be a flat rate, not charged based on distance like Metrorail, Kendall reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

The military has investigated the tragic collision between a Black Hawk helicopter and an American Airlines jet at Reagan National Airport that killed 67 people last year, and determined that there were multiple systemic failures within the Army, The Washington Post reports. Leaders failed to adequately train pilots in navigating DCA’s crowded airspace, failed to collect data on near misses and did not fix flawed helicopter instruments, among other findings.





FROM MARYLAND

All dressed up and nowhere to go: Two Montgomery County high schools have scrapped their homecoming dances because not enough students wanted to go, FOX5 D.C. reports.

“Are you looking for me?” That’s what a 22-year-old University of Maryland student asked a search-and-rescue cruiser after emerging from a six-day disappearance into the woods, The Washington Post reports. He was found Wednesday, and remained in medical care as of yesterday.





METRO MOMENT


Alex Ovechkin AP - 26281016452357 (5725x3817, AR: 1.50)
Alex Ovechkin played his 22nd and final home opener this week, helping the Caps to a 5-3 win over Sidney Crosby and the Penguins. But the best moment of the night came before the puck dropped, when Ovechkin’s two sons, Sergei and Ilya, were given the job of reading off their dad’s name and jersey number. After the game, even Ovechkin — a man of few words and little sentimentality — admitted that he was moved. “It was a pretty cool moment,” he said.

We want to hear from you: Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.





SPORTS

If the NFL season were a football game, the Commanders would have come out flat in the first quarter. Washington is 1-3 after four of its 17 regular season games, a stretch marked by injuries and disappointment. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson and Dave Sheinin took stock of things ahead of Sunday’s Week 5 meeting with the Giants, breaking down the good and the bad from the early weeks of the season.

What to Watch Today

NHL: Capitals vs. Rangers, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Rumble in Grand Rapids
entries.content:
Today’s notice: A memorable night on the debate stage(s). The NRCC chair goes on TV in his own district. On the ground in Alaska and Nevada. And: Following the Freedom 250 money.





THE LATEST

Slugfest Thursday. All you really need to know about a truly astounding debate in Michigan last night: Coming back from the ad break, a frustrated but unflappable Rick Albin, the moderator from WOOD-TV, told viewers, “In 30 years of debates I’ve never seen one continue during the commercials, but it did.”

Supporters of each Senate candidate got plenty to enjoy. Both Republican nominee Mike Rogers and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed landed hits. Each candidate struggled a bit: El-Sayed refused to answer when asked if Iran or Israel is the bigger threat to the U.S. (Both “have proven dangerous in their own way,” he said.)

Rogers’ toughest moments came thanks to Donald Trump. Rogers tried to create distance with the president on tariffs and the Iran war but ended up saying a lot of supportive things about both. After the debate, Rogers told reporters he would welcome a Trump campaign stop in Michigan.

What defined the debate: Name-calling. Rogers called El-Sayed a “con man,” while El-Sayed dubbed Rogers “weak, cowardly.” Rogers did not call his opponent a terrorist, but El-Sayed said he got close enough that he should just “go ahead and say it.” Rogers did not.

It was not the only feisty Senate debate of the night. In Georgia, Republican Rep. Mike Collins needed a big night, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff — the 2026 master of viral lines — was ready. Referring to Collins’ multiple staffing scandals, Ossoff said his opponent had “hired half the Third Reich” to staff his office.

Maine had another Senate debate, and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson again tried to chip away at incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ reputation as an independent voice. She pointed out that Jackson has changed his position evolved over the years on abortion. “Was I voting the wrong way? Yeah,” Jackson said. “But the fact of the matter is that I can admit when I was wrong. Sen. Collins can’t. She still won’t admit that she was wrong in putting Brett Kavanaugh on [the Supreme Court], which took away Roe v. Wade.”

What’s the takeaway from last night? Candidates were prepped and ready, and races like Michigan and Maine remain close after yesterday. But the candidates with the tougher job right now are the Republicans, and on debate stages across the country, they spent more time on defense.

More: Mamdani Tells ICE to Leave New York After an Agent Shot a Man • Pentagon Says Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution Will Be Livestreamed • NYT: Pentagon Draws Up New Iran Strike Plans as Trump Hesitates





FROM NORTH CAROLINA


Uh-oh: The NRCC chair, Rep. Richard Hudson (R-North Carolina), has reserved tens of thousands of dollars in TV ad buys in his own district, The Washington Sun’s Kadia Goba and Chase Pellegrini de Paur report. The district voted Trump +16 in 2024. “Congressman Hudson runs hard every cycle, and this one is no different. He was on air at home in 2022, he was on air in 2024, and he’s on air now,” Hudson’s campaign manager told The Sun. The campaign did not provide documentation suggesting past cycle spending was comparable to the spending his campaign is doing now.

FROM ALASKA


Mary Peltola is confronted over trans rights: The Sun’s Alex Roarty reports from Anchorage, where the Democratic nominee for Senate came face-to-face with backlash over the party’s shift away from trans issues. Peltola is currently running a TV ad pushing back on trans-focused ads run by Republicans. “No, I don’t want kids getting surgeries to change genders or men in girls’ bathrooms,” she says into the camera.

The rhetoric upset a 23 year-old trans man, who confronted Peltola at a campaign stop. He accused Peltola of buying into “a false slander” with the ad and asked the candidate if she planned to support trans rights in the Senate. She did not answer the question directly, Alex writes.

FROM NEVADA


2028 report: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) stumped for Democratic candidates in Nevada this week, which just so happens to be an early state on the party’s 2028 nominating map. The Sun’s Christa Dutton traveled with the pastor for a story about the role faith is playing in so many Democratic campaigns this year. “I think Democrats make a huge mistake when we cede all this ground, when we cede all the terrain around faith and values to Republicans,” he told Christa. “Why would we do that? Especially given the fact that on matters of morality, in my view, they’ve got so much of it wrong.”

FROM THE HILL


Stock buyback fight in defense bill: Major unions are backing a proposal to restrict stock buybacks and dividends by defense contractors in the Senate’s defense policy bill. Major business groups are strongly opposed to the idea. The Sun’s Joe Gould reports on how this argument is scrambling traditional political alliances ahead of the Senate’s return after the midterms.

Where’s the Freedom 250 money? Documents released by a watchdog group yesterday suggest that despite Trump’s promise to fund the nation’s semiquincentennial events through private donations, taxpayers largely footed the bill for the White House’s celebrations. (Reminder: these events were different from the America250 events organized by the commission established by Congress.) The budget estimates leave open questions about where tens of millions in private donations ended up, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.

entries.title: Trump Raised Big Bucks for Freedom 250 — But Most Events Appear to be Funded by Taxpayers
entries.summary: Newly released documents raise questions about what happened to the corporate and private donations.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump touted a tranche of corporate funding for Freedom 250’s private-public partnership to celebrate the semiquincentennial of the nation’s founding. But records obtained and released Thursday by a watchdog group show that taxpayers apparently were who largely supported this summer’s celebrations — raising questions about where tens of millions in private donations ended up.

The Trump administration also has yet to disclose the private sector benefactors themselves, the donation amounts or how tens of millions in funds were spent, despite facing mounting pressure from Democratic lawmakers who allege that some corporate sponsors engaged in a pay-to-play scheme with the federal government.

Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, a nonpartisan group that investigates claims from government employees about environmental misconduct, on Thursday released documents detailing contract agreements and budget calculations for the events.

The official National Park Service charity, the National Park Foundation, helped run the Freedom 250 events.

Its budget estimate, obtained by PEER, showed the events — including the Great American State Fair, the Patriot Games and the Independence Day Celebration at the National Mall — should have cost around $128 million, funded by an expected $100 million from Congress and $14 million in federal grant money specifically for the Mobile Museum, which sent “Freedom Trucks” carrying a curated story of American independence across the country.

The Wall Street Journal reported in August that Freedom 250 raised more than $50 million in private funds and invited donors to a wine reception at the White House in spring 2026. Companies like Chevron, United Airlines and defense conglomerate RTX gave up to several million dollars each to Freedom 250 LLC, based on lobbying disclosures reviewed in July by the nonprofit news organization Sludge, which covers money in politics.

With only $114 million total in expected federal dollars but $128 million in aggregate costs, NPF listed a funding gap of around $14 million at the bottom of the budget chart.

The estimate also did not appear to list any of the $50 million in private donations towards any of the events and celebrations.

Congress received a request from the Interior Department for an additional $10 million in July “to recoup costs associated with support of events celebrating America’s Semiquincentennial,” — though lawmakers did not approve or disburse those additional funds.

“Freedom 250 is proud to have united Americans through unforgettable signature events, nationwide initiatives and projects — from the Freedom Trucks and July 4 celebrations to the 2026 Patriot Games — that celebrate our country and inspire the next generation,” a Freedom 250 spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Sources familiar with planning Freedom 250’s events told The Washington Sun that organizers are still reconciling the event costs and PEER’s documents don’t “represent reality.”

America250, a separate organization established by Congress a decade ago as the official group responsible for planning for the semiquincentennial, reported that it received $25 million of the $100 million the group expected to get in federal funding.

The NPF formally asked NPS to allow it to bypass the traditional competitive bidding process for awarding federal contracts for 250th anniversary-related celebrations, PEER’s documents reveal.

“Due to the immovable national deadlines associated with the 250th anniversary and specific production schedules tied to federal venues and security coordination, time does not permit a full and open competition,” Ruth Hernandez Prescott, NPF’s executive vice president and chief governance officer, wrote in a November 2025 letter addressed to NPS’ acting director.

Prescott added that the “White House has requested engagement of specific qualified contractors with demonstrated capability and security clearances to deliver key components of the commemorative events.”

NPS granted its official charity arm’s request for a waiver to skip the competitive bidding process, citing a timeline concerns and a potential “delay that would be caused by competition.”

entries.title: After Four Games, the Commanders’ Season Is Already on the Brink
entries.summary: A look at the good and the (very) bad from the first quarter of the regular season.
entries.content:
The Washington Commanders arrive at Week 5 with their 2026 season already teetering on the brink. At 1-3 (0-2 in their division) and with injuries having already decimated the roster (23 players were on Wednesday’s injury report), they would have a tough road back into contention even without a brutal upcoming schedule.

But with the resurgent New York Giants coming to Northwest Stadium on Sunday, followed by games against the 49ers, Eagles and Rams, it’s not hard to envision a scenario in which there are no meaningful NFL games in the nation’s capital in the deepest part of winter.

On the other hand, beat the Giants on Sunday, then steal a game or two against that gauntlet — not out of the question so long as quarterback Jayden Daniels can stay on the field — and this season is still salvageable. But that seems like a big ask for a team that is just 6-15 since the 2024 NFC Championship Game.

Here, then, is a big-picture look at where the Commanders stand:

Offense


What has gone right: The Commanders have looked like a legitimate threat with Daniels under center, nearly stealing their season-opener at Philadelphia, then driving up and down the field at Dallas until Daniels dislocated his elbow on the final play of the first half. While veteran Marcus Mariota was a more-than-serviceable fill-in, leading the team to a (temporarily) season-saving upset of the Seattle Seahawks in Week 3, he, too, was lost to an injury (strained MCL), forcing third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis into action during Washington’s loss to Indianapolis in London last week. With Daniels expected to return Sunday, the crisis at quarterback appears to be over, at least for now.

Elsewhere, third-round rookie Antonio Williams has been a revelation at wideout, catching a touchdown against the Eagles and seeing an apparent 87-yard touchdown against the Colts called back due to a penalty, while veteran Stefon Diggs (18 catches, three touchdowns) has been a solid offseason pickup (though his unsportsmanlike conduct penalty in Week 1 cost the team dearly).

While the offensive line has been in flux (more below), left tackle Josh Conerly Jr. and center Lucas Patrick have been surprise standouts. The pair have combined to allow zero sacks and two hits on the quarterback, even with Patrick having not played regularly at center since 2021.

What has gone wrong: If you had been asked at the start of training camp to name the three most important figures on the Commanders’ offense, you likely would have said Daniels, wide receiver Terry McLaurin and left tackle Laremy Tunsil. All three have already missed games due to injury, with Tunsil (torn triceps) likely out for the season. And it’s never a good sign when three different quarterbacks have finished your first four games.

In some ways, the offensive line has never recovered from the loss of Tunsil or the decision to release former Pro Bowl center Tyler Biadasz (or sign a suitable replacement). The resulting shuffle of personnel — Washington has started two different players at center and three different players at right guard in four weeks — has highlighted the Commanders’ lack of depth, especially after the mysterious Week 4 benching of veteran Nick Allegretti, whose replacement, sixth-round rookie Matt Gulbin, was exposed at right guard by the Colts’ DeForest Buckner. Brandon Coleman, Tunsil’s replacement at left tackle, has also struggled, allowing a team-high 14 quarterback pressures so far.

In an undoubtedly related development, Commanders tight ends have been virtually invisible in the passing game, combining for just 10 catches for 65 yards through the first four games — despite the signing of veteran Chig Okonkwo this offseason. Okonkwo, who has three 50-catch seasons on his resume, has just four catches in two games, missing the Cowboys and Seahawks games with a hamstring injury. This lack of production has particularly harmed the offense on third downs, with the Commanders’ 31.6% success rate ranking 30th in the NFL.

Coming into the season, new offensive coordinator David Blough harped on generating explosive plays, defined as rushes of 10 or more yards and receptions of 20 or more yards. That just hasn’t happened through the first four games: Washington has created explosives on just 4.2% of their plays, according to Sharp Football Analysis. That’s the fourth-worst rate in the league.

What awaits: With Daniels back at quarterback and right guard Sam Cosmi (concussion) nearing his return, there is still hope the offense can regain the explosiveness it has shown at times in the first part of the season. But the defenses of the Giants, 49ers and Rams are all ranked in the top 10 in the NFL in both points and total yards allowed, and the Eagles (though they are underperforming this season) are perennially elite.

Amik Robertson AP - 26277655706742 (3443x2295, AR: 1.50)

Defense


What has gone right: There have been moments of brilliance from the defense from week to week and player to player. The Commanders didn’t allow a rushing touchdown until the Colts’ Jonathan Taylor found the end zone twice in Week 4, and many of the newcomers to this unit have lived up to their hype and then some. That includes: edge rusher Odafe Oweh, who has been a constant menace to opposing quarterbacks; rookie linebacker Sonny Styles, who already has one NFC Defensive Player of the Week honor; and defensive backs Amik Robertson, Nick Cross and Rasul Douglas, who have been bright spots within their otherwise embattled unit. After failing to generate a turnover in the first two games, the defense has forced five in the past two.

What has gone wrong: The inconsistency on defense from game to game, or even quarter to quarter, has been maddening at times, as epitomized in the Week 4 loss to the Colts: Indianapolis’ first five drives went fumble, punt, punt, punt, interception; their next seven went touchdown, field goal, touchdown, field goal, punt, touchdown, field goal. Through four games, the Commanders allowed the most second-half points (17.8) in the league and were outscored 43-29 in the fourth quarter. Injuries have begun compounding, particularly at linebacker, where veterans Frankie Luvu and Leo Chenal both missed the Colts game, with the latter now on injured reserve following neck surgery.

The unit as a whole has been dangerously susceptible to big plays, which helps explain how the Commanders can rank 18th in the NFL in yards allowed per game but 30th in points allowed per game. The failure to keep opponents out of the end zone is perhaps best illustrated by the fact opposing offenses have scored touchdowns on 80% of their red zone possessions, which ranks 30th in the NFL. Cornerback Mikey Sainristil was a big part of the problem, losing his starting role after Week 2 and playing just five defensive snaps against the Colts.

What awaits: The run defense will face a particularly strong test in the coming weeks, with the Giants, 49ers, Eagles and Rams all ranking in the upper half in rushing yards per game through four games. But it will catch a break against the Giants, whose starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, is out for the season, leaving their offense in the hands of veteran Jameis Winston. If cornerback Trey Amos (ankle) is activated from injured reserve this week, that could be a huge boost for the Commanders’ secondary.

entries.title: Warnock Leans on Faith to Boost Democrats — And Maybe His Own Presidential Ambitions
entries.summary: The Georgia senator, campaigning in the early nominating state of Nevada, said he wants his party to stop ceding “faith and values” to Republicans.
entries.content:
LAS VEGAS — On stage at a gathering of faith leaders here this week, Sen. Raphael Warnock told the crowd how he sees the midterms: “This is not just a political happening, but a spiritual undertaking.”

The senator and pastor campaigned across the city on Wednesday to boost his party in this year's election, making an argument hinged on faith that might shape his party for the next one.

Nevada has rapidly become a gathering spot for the growing congregation of Democrats considering a presidential run. In just the last few days, Pete Buttigieg and Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) traveled to what will be one of Democrats’ first nominating states in 2028, making a point of campaigning for the Democratic gubernatorial candidate as well as linking up with local unions.

Warnock left his own options open in an interview with The Washington Sun on Wednesday. Asked how his role as a pastor is informing any decisions about 2028, he said the country is at “an inflection point.”

“But this is so much larger than the cycle,” he said. “This is really about the character of the country, and it's a big and important conversation. And I look forward to participating in that conversation."

Warnock, who is pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, wants to be a “countervailing witness of what faith looks like in public” and said his party needs to do more to center faith.

“I think Democrats make a huge mistake when we cede all this ground, when we cede all the terrain around faith and values to Republicans,” Warnock said. “Why would we do that? Especially given the fact that on matters of morality, in my view, they've got so much of it wrong.”

At the same time, his party is struggling with many faith groups. The country also faces questions of purpose as artificial intelligence poses an uncertain future and loneliness continues to rise.

“We are drowning in a sea of loneliness and hyperconnectivity. That's the irony of the moment,” Warnock told The Sun. While the decline of mainline Christianity preceded AI, a yearning for connection is not declining, he said.

“That creates a real opportunity for faith leaders and principled leaders in the political space to bring people together to address huge problems that confront us to deal with both the perils and the promises of AI, because it's not going anywhere,” he said.

Other politicians are also leaning into their faith this election year, like James Talarico, a seminary student running for Senate in Texas, and Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor running for Senate in Kansas. Both states, once long-shots for Democrats, are now in play.

Warnock also emphasized his faith in a crowded get-out-the-vote rally in Nevada’s 4th Congressional District — where Democratic Rep. Steven Horsford is running for reelection — by launching into a speech fusing religion and politics.

It came alongside a vivid denunciation of the current Republican Party. He shared a memory from his childhood in which his grandmother chopped the head off a snake in the garden. He said he was frightened because the snake started moving sporadically.

“I didn't understand that his animated movements, his exaggerated movements, were happening not because he was living, but because he was dying,” Warnock told the crowd.

“He preachin’,” Horsford interjected.

“As you witness them doing crazy, desperate things, as you witness them trying to pass the SAVE Act, as you witness the cruelty and brutality of ICE, as you witness what Donald Trump is trying to do, as you witness folks close rank and try to buy this election, it is because they know that that old order, that old racist, misogynistic, homophobic, xenophobic order, is on its way out,” Warnock said to applause.

Warnock has regularly derided Republicans who invoke faith as they make policy decisions that he considers out of line with the Scriptures. Calling that out is a “service to the country,” he told The Sun.

Last week, Warnock criticized Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth for using the words of the Old Testament prophet Isaiah — “Here I am Lord, send me” — to commend and recruit military officers. He has also criticized Speaker of the House Mike Johnson for praying before passing the reconciliation bill last summer.

“They pray before they kick 15 million people off of their health care. They pray before they kick children off SNAP. They pray before they double people's health care premiums,” Warnock said at the faith leaders event.

Democrats are lagging Republicans in support from some of the biggest religious groups in the U.S. A majority of Protestants and Catholics align with the Republican Party, Pew Research has found, while Democrats overperform with people who claim no religion.

“A lot of the people I know that claim to be Christian seem to be getting less of Christianity and more of — I don't know what it is — it’s politics, really,” said retired artist Linda Overbey at the rally in Horsford’s office. She came to the rally because she is a Warnock fan. “He represents the good to me.”

Warnock is aware of how some voters have come to view religion as a way to exert power, and is careful not to prescribe anything approaching a theocracy.

“I love this grand experiment of a multifaceted, multiracial, multi-religious republic, where people of various faith traditions and those who claim no faith tradition at all are in covenant with one another,” he said in an interview at the Service Employees International Union Nevada Local 1107 headquarters after a roundtable with union members.

He commended Nevada for representing that grand experiment as he looked around the get-out-the-vote rally in the 4th District.

“This looks like the kingdom of God,” he said. “This is God's dream for the world.”

entries.title: Mamdani Tells ICE to Leave New York After an Agent Shot a Man
entries.summary: DHS said the man was wounded while immigration agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation.”
entries.content:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to leave New York City after police say a federal immigration agent shot and wounded a man in front of his 5-year-old son.

An ICE agent fired seven rounds into a car, striking 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the neck below his left ear, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a press conference Thursday night. The child inside the car is safe and with a family member, Tisch said.

Belgal was treated at a hospital but Mamdani said ICE removed him just before the press conference.

"For the past two hours, I have been on the phone with President [Donald] Trump and [Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne] Mullin, negotiating the release of the man ICE agents shot,” Mamdani said Thursday night. “Those negotiations were unsuccessful. Just moments ago, ICE put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away."

In the hours after the shooting, the mayor, in an X post, called to “abolish ICE” and labeled the event “unconscionable.”

The Department of Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that ICE agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” when an officer “discharged his weapon” and injured a man, who the department said was an unauthorized immigrant from the Dominican Republic.

Belgal has two prior arrests in New York City. He received five years probation for a robbery in 2023 and has a pending case for criminal sale of a controlled substance, Tisch said.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said on X that she had spoken with Trump and Mullin but did not say whether they had committed to her requests to halt immigration enforcement operations in the state.

Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-New York) said on X that ICE denied him access from Belgal’s hospital room. The man’s family was also denied visitation, Espaillat said.

Hochul said she expected federal officials to “provide a full and transparent accounting” of the shooting. Espaillat demanded in a post on X that all footage be preserved and unaltered.

The White House referred The Sun to DHS’s statement.

This story has been updated with further information from city officials’ press conference.

entries.title: Trump Is Renewing His Effort to Oust the Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook
entries.summary: The president established a “committee of inquiry” into the Federal Reserve governor.
entries.content:
By Christopher Rugaber

President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.

The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn't be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.

Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve's independence as the president demands the central bank cut its key interest rate. Just last month, the Fed raised its key rate instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.

Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed's broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for the rate hike. Cook is one of the 12 participants on the committee that votes on interest-rate decisions. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous.

The move follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from “trying again” as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.

Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.

entries.title: ICE Agents Were Wearing Body Cameras in Marble Hill Shooting, Mullin Says
entries.summary: The Homeland Security secretary focused his comments about the shooting on the man’s criminal history, calling him a “thug.”
entries.content:
Federal immigration agents who shot a man Thursday with his 5-year-old son in the car in New York City were wearing body cameras that were turned on, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday.

Oscar Belgal, 28, is in federal immigration custody and has already been taken out of New York state into a highly secure facility, Mullin said during a press conference Friday morning. Mullin declined to say where Belgal, an undocumented immigrant from the Dominican Republic, is being held.

“Unfortunately, we are giving so much attention to this thug that was a true threat to society to the point that we had to put him into a more secure facility outside of New York,” Mullin said.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference Thursday night that he had spoken with President Donald Trump and Mullin repeatedly, but that efforts to obtain Belgal’s release from ICE custody had been unsuccessful.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot Belgal in the neck in Marble Hill, a neighborhood in northern Manhattan.

The ICE agent shot seven rounds into the car while Belgal’s 5-year-old son was inside, New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Thursday night, and Belgal was hospitalized shortly after the shooting.

Mullin on Friday blamed Belgal for putting the child in danger and accused him of trying to weaponize his car, a claim Trump administration officials have used to justify previous incidents of immigration officers shooting at people.

“Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life, and the life of their partners and general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons,” Mullin said.

Agents tried to take Belgal into custody in September but did not pursue him after he fled, Mullin said. The shooting is being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Federal Bureau of Investigations, Mullin confirmed.

Belgal was backing into a parking spot when a plainclothes ICE agent approached the driver’s side window with his gun drawn, Tisch said, describing NYPD surveillance camera footage. Other agents approached the car from the driver’s headlight and Belgal moved the car forward outside of the camera’s view, which did not capture the shooting, she said.

Mullin focused his comments on Belgal’s criminal history. Belgal has two prior arrests in New York City, received five years probation for a robbery in 2023 and has a pending case for criminal sale of a controlled substance, Tisch said.

Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-New York) said he met with the child and the child’s mother in the hospital Thursday. ICE agents blocked Espaillat and the family from visiting Belgal, the lawmaker said.

“The child is in good health but obviously traumatized by this whole ordeal,” Espaillat told The Washington Sun.

Espaillat said the ICE agents approached the enforcement operation in a dangerous manner, with an agent brandishing a gun.

“There's heavy foot traffic there,” the lawmaker said. “There are schools around there, and this was about 4 p.m, so it's a time where children and families are walking around the neighborhood.”

entries.title: The New-Look Wizards Made a Good First Impression in Their Preseason Opener
entries.summary: AJ Dybantsa, Anthony Davis and Trae Young all played in a win over the Knicks.
entries.content:
NEW YORK — AJ Dybantsa remains undefeated at Madison Square Garden.

A year after rallying BYU to a come-from-behind win against Clemson at the storied arena, Dybantsa and the new-look Wizards won their preseason opener 111–109 over the defending champion Knicks on Thursday night.

“I told everyone coming here I was 1-0,” Dybantsa said after the game. “I just wanted to come in and go 2-0, which I did.”

NBA preseason games aren’t much different from those in the NFL: The starters only play so much, and the players who log the most minutes may not be guaranteed a roster spot. But for a team that had yet to see Dybantsa against NBA competition or star duo Anthony Davis and Trae Young play together, Thursday’s preseason opener held some importance for the Wizards.

“It’s good to finally get a game under our belt,” Dybantsa said of playing with Davis and Young. “See what we can do out there.”

Here are some first impressions from Thursday night:

Davis showed no rust after a long layoff.

Thursday was Davis’ first game in nine months, after he injured his hand in January and didn’t see the court after being traded to the Wizards in February. Despite the long layoff, he didn’t show any rust. Davis hit his first three shots, including a pair of 3s, and finished with a game-high 16 points in just under 17 minutes.

“I thought he was terrific,” Wizards coach Brian Keefe said of Davis. “Anchoring our defense, his communication, his ability to zone up on the back side and then you saw just his efficiency on the offensive end. He’s going to settle us down when we play through the post because he’s so comfortable down there.”

Keefe started Davis alongside Deandre Ayton, which allowed him to play power forward, his preferred position. The Wizards also used lineups with Davis as the center, and it’s easy to see Alex Sarr joining the rotation once he’s healthy and allow Davis to play both positions during a game. Ayton grabbed a game-high 10 rebounds while Davis added seven.

“They controlled the game defensively,” Keefe said of his bigs. “You saw the rebounding by Deandre. We wanted to establish our size and physicality.”

Young played well both on and off the ball. 

While the Knicks entered Thursday off their first championship season in 53 years, Young is coming off one in which he played just 15 games after requesting a trade out of Atlanta and battling injuries.

But his status as a Knicks villain remains unchanged. Young was promptly booed after being introduced Thursday, and on the court he reminded fans why they dislike him so. He scored 15 points in 17 minutes, dished out four assists and added a pair of steals. Young went 3 for 6 from behind the arc. He shot one triple on one foot, which Wizards assistant Patrick Ewing might have an opinion on.

https://x.com/washwizards/status/2108349495117295816?s=46&t=oKtVAS4CgKYhV-P9_DfngQ
Young started the game off the ball as Kyshawn George initiated the Wizards offense off the opening tip and had a game-high five assists. But Keefe played Young both on and off the ball and gave him extended run with the reserves as he led the second unit as a scorer and a playmaker.

“We’ve got a lot of guys who can make decisions,” Keefe said. “We think that’s going to be the best way forward for us to reach where we want to go to. He’s just so unselfish. Kicking the ball ahead. Looking for his teammates, that stuff just brings energy to your team.”

Dybantsa settled in and provided a few highlights. 

The No. 1 pick had a rough start to the preseason, missing his first few shows from the field. But he got better as the game went on, stuffing the stat sheet and showing why teams spent the past year hoping for a shot at his services.

Dybantsa finished with 11 points on 5 for 11 shooting and added a pair of rebounds and assists. He missed all three attempts from 3. Defensively, he was a pest, using his 7-foot wingspan to deflect passes and disrupt the Knicks offense.

https://x.com/washwizards/status/2108354220118135059?s=46&t=oKtVAS4CgKYhV-P9_DfngQ
“The biggest thing I thought with him was that he had four steals,” Keefe said. “His effort on the defensive end, cutting people off, playing in the passing lanes, and then you saw him getting out in transition, getting easy baskets. Pretty good first showing.”

Dybantsa admitted he felt sped-up early on as he adjusted to the pace of the NBA. He said playing alongside Ayton and Davis allowed him to be more aggressive defensively because he knew he had two centers behind him if he got beat.

In addition to the defense and scoring, Dybantsa showed some playmaking ability, too. Knicks wing OG Anunoby started on Dybantsa, and the rookie held his own against one of the NBA’s best defenders. In the first quarter, Dybantsa drove on Anunoby and threw a pretty lob to George.

https://x.com/WashWizards/status/2108355859562533295“There’s going to be a lot of opportunities where I can get easy assists if I just slow down a little bit,” Dybantsa said of his performance. “And defensively, just play without fouling. There was a couple of dumb fouls I got.”

One more note: The Wizards were without four players Thursday, but Keefe expects that number to drop to two in the near future. Sarr sat out as he continues to recover from a fractured foot, which occurred in a June workout, and Khris Middleton didn’t play as he continues to ramp-up as well, but Keefe said both players are on pace to play in the preseason. Jamir Watkins (ACL recovery) and Tristan Vukčević (hip) were also out.

entries.title: How a ‘Hornet’s Nest’ of Angry Texans Is Fighting Trump’s Big Bend Border Wall
entries.summary: “Landowner resistance has slowed this project to a crawl,” said David Keller, a landowner suing to stop the plans.
entries.content:
By Rebecca Santana

RUIDOSA, Texas (AP) — The message from the Trump administration has been clear: It is moving ahead with a $46 billion border wall project stretching from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

But in Texas’ Big Bend region, the administration has run up against intense opposition from landowners, many of whom are unwilling to cede parts of their property for what they see as a waste of taxpayer dollars.

That resistance is complicating President Donald Trump’s signature infrastructure project in a fight that has become a test of just how far the administration will go to fulfill its vision of a fortified southern border.

The administration has committed billions of dollars and waived environmental and other protections to plow ahead with the project despite the region’s historically low illegal crossings, its formidable natural barriers and a surge of bipartisan opposition that has scrambled traditional border politics.

The federal government has sweeping authority to force the project through. But a judge has now paused construction across the region, giving a major boost to landowners who have sought to impede the wall by refusing to cooperate with government surveyors, protesting at county meetings and gearing up for court battles.

“Landowner resistance has slowed this project to a crawl,” said David Keller, a landowner suing to stop the Big Bend border plans. The administration, he added, was “woefully unprepared for the hornet’s nest they stirred up.”

Trump has long pledged to build the border wall

Building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has long been a key campaign promise for Trump. And the administration pushed ahead with it after Republicans last year approved $46 billion for the border wall as part of a sweeping immigration enforcement package.

Although illegal crossings have plummeted under Trump, the administration says walls, vehicle barriers, surveillance technology and patrol roads are needed to keep them low.

Customs and Border Protection says it’s building an average of about 12 miles or 20 kilometers of barrier a week and had recently hit a milestone of more than 200 miles (320 km) of new walls built under the second Trump administration.

In Big Bend, where construction began in September, the administration plans to spend $7.5 billion to fortify the border along a region stretching more than 500 miles (800 km).

In August, the Border Patrol arrested 8,870 people along the southern border. In Big Bend, which makes up roughly one quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border, it arrested 161.

“The American people have already seen the consequences of an unprotected border," said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott after a lawsuit filed by landowners against the Big Bend project. “We cannot allow any region — including Big Bend — to be exploited again.”

Landowners gird for court battles

Unlike in other border areas, much of the land in Texas is privately or state owned.

The government must acquire authorization from owners to survey and build and if they refuse, can take them to court. The process by which the government takes someone’s property for public use in exchange for compensation is known as eminent domain and courts generally defer to the government in these cases.

That hasn't stopped Dianna and Dan Burbach.

The Burbachs began receiving paperwork in July seeking permission to survey their property, along with a map showing where the project would run behind their house. An August letter said the government had an “immediate need” to enter and warned that it could go to court within 90 days.

Dianna, 63, and her husband, 79, arrived 25 years ago and raised four children in their orange adobe house on property stretching to the Rio Grande. Now retired, they worry construction could worsen flooding and leave 15 acres (6 hectares) of their land behind the wall.

“We’re going to let them take us to court, do eminent domain," Dianna said. "We’ll fight it that way.”

A Justice Department official said CBP has reached agreements with dozens of Big Bend landowners but that the administration has hired eminent domain attorneys in Texas in anticipation of the disputes. Across the southern border, about 70 such cases have been referred to the department during Trump’s second term, and 50 have already been resolved — none required going to trial, said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the government.

The No Big Bend Wall Coalition, which says its network includes more than 200 landowners, recently sued to block construction. The plaintiffs argue that Homeland Security is misusing its authority in a region with little illegal cross-border activity.

Lawsuits aiming to stop or slow the border wall projects have largely been unsuccessful. But in a major win for opponents, a federal judge temporarily barred wall construction in the Big Bend area. Plaintiffs argued the administration had overstepped its congressional authority by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass environmental and other regulations.

Keller said the judge’s ruling was “unqualified good news” but uncertainty over its future meant the landowners would continue their fight.

It’s not immediately clear how long the judge’s order will slow the government, which late Thursday asked the judge to put aside her order while they appeal.

The administration also argued in the court filing that leaving segments along the border without adequate border security infrastructure could lead to a funnel effect where illegal immigration or smuggling would flow to the area that was least fortified — specifically the Big Bend region.

Protesting contractors and lobbying local officials

Other opponents are pressing local governments not to assist contractors. Charlie Angell, a tourism operator notified that the government wanted access to his land for the border project, and his partner, Bibiana Gutierrez, attend county meetings throughout the region.

They and other land and business owners have staged protests, patrolled areas where contractors are working to look for possible violations, and hung signs telling contractors they’re not welcome at local hotels or restaurants.

In Terrell County, residents unsuccessfully urged officials not to lease airport land to a barrier contractor. In Jeff Davis County, a proposed agreement allowing another contractor to use a county road has so far not been approved.

The financial incentives for some of these cash-starved counties are clear and some local officials have argued they have little leverage on a federal plan.

“We’re not in control of the border wall. We’re not,” Terrell County Judge Dale Lynn Carruthers told a room crowded with people who had come to speak out against the airport lease. She said if they didn't lease the land, the contractor would just buy it elsewhere. “We’re just a little old Terrell County.”

But Angell and Gutierrez argue that the local opposition has more strength than some might realize.

“If we had rolled over, the wall would be up,” Gutierrez said.

CBP said it continues seeking voluntary access agreements while completing the project’s design but will refer disputes to the Justice Department when necessary. Landowners will be compensated regardless of how access is obtained, the agency said.

The opposition has bipartisan support

After a yearslong surge in crossings at the southern frontier, border security and immigration were key reasons Republicans voted for Trump and his approval ratings on those issues are among his strongest.

But with illegal crossings plummeting, even some Republicans who voted for Trump on the issue of border security have questioned the need for the multi-billion dollar infrastructure through Big Bend.

Local sheriffs opposed the project early, and bulldozing in Big Bend National Park prompted Republican Sen. John Cornyn to press Homeland Security about Texans’ concerns.

Laura Allen, a Republican rancher who voted for Trump twice, is now receiving notices that a vehicle barrier will cross the property where her family raises sheep and goats. She credits Trump with shutting down the border but says spending billions on barriers in Big Bend is unnecessary.

“I didn’t vote for a wall,” she said. “I wanted our border secured. He accomplished that.”

Terrell County’s Republican sheriff, Thad Cleveland, who spent 26 years in the Border Patrol, is among those speaking out against the project in Big Bend. He said that in the rugged county he polices, drones and surveillance towers make more sense than a wall to find and stop illegal border crossers.

“We have the advantage of time and distance out here,” he said.

The land itself is a natural deterrent, critics say

In some areas, the river is flanked on both sides by steep limestone cliffs, and up and down the region, people have to trek through inhospitable desert terrain to get to the nearest paved road or pass through Border Patrol checkpoints.

Reaching Gary Grabowske’s land requires grinding along rocky mountain trails and through gullies carved by flash floods. From the top of a 450-foot cliff (137 meters), the Rio Grande is visible far below. There is no electricity, running water or internet and, Grabowske argues, no plausible route for a vehicle entering from Mexico.

“You can’t take a dirt bike to the bottom," said Grabowske, gesturing to the canyon below. “You can’t take a mule to the bottom. You’re scrambling down there, hand over fist.” He added: “There’s no vehicle in the world that could cross any of this.”

Opponents say the fight reaches beyond whether a wall makes sense in Big Bend. They see it as a test of how far the federal government can go when landowners stand in the way of one of its priorities.

“We’re a pretty tough bunch,” said Allen. “But if we’re going to be run over and have our land taken by our own government, what makes anybody else in this United States think that they’re exempt?”

Ranchers try to resist

The Zuberbueler ranch in Val Verde County was founded in 1898. Brothers Bill and Patrick own and lease thousands of acres of the craggy land stretching to the river. Their Angora goats and Rambouillet sheep roam over the land, stopping at a network of water troughs.

Bill remembers when, back in February, he first got the letter giving him five days to respond to a request to access his property for construction and raising the possibility of the government using eminent domain. He worries about how the construction will affect his livestock, especially their water supply. And while his animals could pass through the vehicle barriers, the cowboys herding them could not.

“There’s not a lot of grass out here, but every square foot is important to my bottom line,” said Bill.

They have so far refused to allow anyone onto their land to survey or build. They feel the weight of their family’s legacy and the sacrifices previous generations made to build the ranch up.

“Regardless of what happens, we have to say we tried,” said Patrick.

Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.
