entries.title: FBI Is Angling to Hand the UFC a No-Bid Contract to Train Agents
entries.summary: The contract would expand an existing partnership between the Trump administration and the UFC.
entries.content:
The FBI wants to hire the Ultimate Fighting Championship to train its special agents under a one-year deal that would bypass the competitive bidding process typically used for federal contracts, according to federal records.

The agency claimed that the UFC is the only organization qualified to provide the training within its required time frame. The estimated cost of the proposed deal was redacted from the publicly released documents.

The contract would expand an existing partnership between FBI Director Kash Patel and the UFC, which is led by Dana White, a longtime friend and ally of President Donald Trump.

In March, UFC fighters visited the FBI Academy in Quantico, Virginia, for a two-day training seminar. Patel praised the collaboration at the time, calling it a "tremendous opportunity" for agents to learn from elite athletes.

In June, the UFC staged a major fighting event on the White House South Lawn, attended by Trump and White.

Rob D’Amico, a former member of the FBI's Hostage Rescue Team who also taught defensive tactics, accused Patel of “trying to give his friend Dana White a lucrative contract,” during a Friday interview with MS NOW.

He also called the idea that UFC was the only, or even the best, organization capable of training FBI agents ridiculous.

In a justification published Sept. 30, the FBI said it had researched other training providers but found none capable of delivering the full range of fighting techniques it wanted.

The agency also acknowledged that no other companies had expressed interest because the contract had not been advertised when the justification was prepared.

The proposed training would take place at the FBI Academy in Quantico and cover techniques including striking, grappling, takedowns, weapon defense and ground control.

The FBI said the one-year arrangement would give it time to research other providers before opening a longer-term contract to competition. The notice lists an Oct. 15 deadline for responses. It does not establish that a contract has been awarded.

Patel first floated the idea of bringing UFC fighters into the bureau's training program shortly after taking office in February 2025.

The March training included prominent UFC fighters Justin Gaethje, Jorge Masvidal and Chris Weidman.

entries.title: The Commanders’ Tight Ends Haven’t Produced, but the Issue Is Not as It Seems
entries.summary: Through four games, Washington has had the league’s least-productive tight ends unit.
entries.content:
Chig Okonkwo was standing by himself with the closest Eagle nearly 15 yards upfield.

Had the Commanders’ tight end been seen and targeted, he likely would have created one of the explosive plays that he’s most known for and that offensive coordinator David Blough has emphasized this season. Instead, Philadelphia’s pass rush got to Jayden Daniels, and the quarterback had to run for his life around the pocket before tossing the ball out of bounds in what would be a Week 1 loss.

Washington’s tight ends — John Bates, Ben Sinnott, Colson Yankoff and Okonkwo — have combined to produce just 10 receptions, 65 yards and zero touchdowns through the first four weeks of the season, the least-productive group in the NFL.

Multiple factors have contributed to the unit’s lack of success, but none as simple as “they don’t get open.” And for a passing offense that ranks 24th in the league, the 1-3 Commanders need this group to get going if they’re going to salvage a season that is quickly spiraling.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“For our entire unit, it's consistency and execution,” Blough said recently. “Wanting to see the play style continue to improve, and as we build on this thing as we go throughout the entire season, just continue to see the consistent improvement in [the tight ends] room and the opportunities will certainly come, and we're working on that.”

But some opportunities have already passed. Okonkwo, who ranked sixth among tight ends in yards after catch last season, has been wide open on more than a handful of the 48 routes he’s run this season. (He missed two games due to a hamstring injury.) Pressure on the quarterback has prevented the ball from getting to him.

On the aforementioned Eagles play from Week 1, a flea-flicker play call was almost immediately blown up by defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.

Commanders tight ends 1 (1376x767, AR: 1.79)
Later in the game on a third-and-10, Okonkwo had space on a quick slant, but the Eagles were again barreling down on Daniels, forcing him to bomb it down the field to receiver Dyami Brown before getting popped.

In Week 4 against the Colts, Okonkwo had one play where he was running free on a deep corner route. But just as third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis spotted him, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner put his helmet in the quarterback’s chest, forcing the ball to sail over Okonkwo’s head and nearly into the hands of safety A.J. Haulcy.

But that’s not to say the tight ends, and Blough, aren’t culpable. While Okonkwo and Yankoff have found openings in the defense, Bates and Sinnott have struggled to create separation.

“We're just doing what we're asked to do and owning that,” Sinnott said. “And when those opportunities come, we're just looking to take advantage of it.”

Blough has shown the ability to scheme open his tight ends, but the results haven’t yet played out on the field. Against the Colts, receiver Stefon Diggs ran a rub route, with the intention of throwing off Okonkwo’s defender. In theory, it would have freed Okonkwo up the left side of the field for a sizable gain.

The only problem was the defender, linebacker Jaylon Carlies, ran around Diggs without breaking his stride. Instead of Okonkwo finding daylight, Carlies was able to bring him down for just a 2-yard gain.

Commanders tight ends 2 (1376x708, AR: 1.94)
There have been times Blough has found a way to use the tight ends even if they’re not getting the ball, using them to drag linebackers and defensive backs away from other pass-catchers. Okonkwo ran a go route against the Colts that took Carlies and corner Sauce Gardner out of the flat, where running back Bill Croskey-Merritt was able to take a dump-off for a 35-yard gain.

“It’s a bunch of ‘if, ands,’” Yankoff said. “If you tie him down and he bites on you, that means this guy’s open. That’s a win in our book.”

Righting the ship in Week 5 may prove difficult, as the Giants defense hasn’t been forgiving to tight ends. New York uses safeties in man coverage to force tight ends to beat one-on-one matchups, which has led to just two tight ends (the Rams’ Terrance Ferguson and Cardinals’ Trey McBride) gaining 20 or more yards on them in a game. Ferguson is the lone tight end to score a touchdown against New York.

But the difference on Sunday will be the presence of Daniels, who missed the last two games with a dislocated left elbow. Right guard Sam Cosmi, out for a concussion, will also return from a two-game absence, helping to shore up some of the pressure problems Washington has faced. Okonkwo and Daniels spent a lot of time working together over the summer, but injuries to both have prevented them from gelling on the field.

While Daniels said his focus is “to get the ball to the open guy,” Okonkwo is more bullish on the results he and the other tight ends can produce going forward.

“I know how it goes. Some games you might not get the rock, and some games the ball keeps finding you,” Okonkwo said. “I don't panic … I know what I can do. I know what Jayden can do. When we get on the field and do it together, everybody will see it, and then everything will be put to bed at that point.”

entries.title: Arlington County Sues to Block Construction of Trump’s Massive Arch
entries.summary: The lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of not properly evaluating the monument's potential harm.
entries.content:
Arlington County is suing to stop the construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed Triumphal Arch, arguing the administration failed to complete a legally required environmental review process before barreling ahead with the development.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Virginia, alleges the Trump administration did not properly evaluate the project’s potential harm or offer meaningful alternatives as required by the National Environmental Policy Act. The complaint seeks to halt construction work until a proper environmental review is conducted.

Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch is slated to be built at Memorial Circle on an island in the Potomac River that sits within the borders of D.C. but is adjacent to Arlington.

The National Park Service, which oversees projects on federal parkland including the arch, “has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process,” the lawsuit said. “That rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President’s repeated marching orders.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

A previous study from the Park Service found the monument will likely disturb dozens of historic sites, including Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington Memorial Bridge. Another said the arch will narrow the visual field of the area, cause temporary traffic interruptions and create noise near memorials and the cemetery. Still, the Park Service said the arch should proceed as planned because the location is “central to the undertaking” of the project.

Trump has championed the arch as a monument to honor the nation’s 250th birthday. Last month he said it would also serve as a “top grade military complex” housing drones, snipers and ammunition. Trump has used similar rationale to garner support for other beautification projects, such as the White House ballroom, which he touted as necessary for national security.

The lawsuit filed by Arlington County comes amid another ongoing legal battle surrounding the arch. A group of Vietnam veterans sued in February to stop the monument, arguing it would disrupt the view of Arlington National Cemetery.

The arch has also drawn criticism from aviation experts who worry the massive structure will make already congested airspace near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport more dangerous.

Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement Thursday the federal government disregarded protocol and wide-ranging negative impacts that the arch will bring to Arlington County.

“Our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project,” he said. “Enough is enough. We will do all we can to hold this administration accountable and to protect and serve the best interests of our community.”

The arch received an early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, a board packed with Trump appointees. Final approval could come as early as Nov. 5, when the project is expected to be presented to the National Capital Planning Commission.

entries.title: Moderate Democrats Propose Banning Pocket Rescissions Once and For All
entries.summary: Democrats’ response to Trump’s takeover of government spending is beginning to take shape.
entries.content:
Moderate Democrats want Congress to wrest back some control over government spending from the president.

Their proposal: a major overhaul of the budget process that would impose new limitations on the White House.

A new bill introduced on Friday by the Blue Dog Coalition would end pocket rescissions, the process through which President Donald Trump rescinded more than $800 million in already appropriated funds, according to bill text shared exclusively with The Washington Sun.

“It feels like once some weasel finds a new trick to outmaneuver congressional intent, that can become standard, and you know, [there is] the importance of saying we’re gonna hold the line here,” said Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Washington), a co-sponsor of the bill. “We will exert our status as a co-equal branch.”

The bill, called the Congressional Budget Reform Act, is one example of how Democrats are looking to hold the president accountable should they win back the majority in the midterms. Democrats and Republicans alike have expressed their frustration about the Trump administration undermining Congress’ power of the purse, but the Republican majority has largely rubber stamped the White House’s actions.

Bill sponsor Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), who is not running for reelection, said lawmakers’ concerns about the budget process increases the likelihood that they prioritize the issue as they plan next year’s agenda during the lame-duck period.

“Congress has been, in a bipartisan way, protective of the power of the purse,” Golden said in an interview with The Sun. “There will be an appetite for some of these things about impoundments, rescissions.”

The Blue Dog bill would prohibit the Office of Management and Budget from requesting rescissions or withholding funds within 90 days of a line item’s expiration.

The Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 says the president can temporarily hold funds for up to 45 days while Congress reviews the rescission request. The Trump administration has attempted to subvert Congress’ role by submitting these rescissions for review so close to the funds’ expiration date that Congress doesn’t have the full 45 days to act. The Government Accountability Office has concluded that practice goes against the law.

“Congress is in no way helpless in any of this. … They have the spending power and they just have to have the votes in order to wield it,” said Devin O’Connor, a senior federal fiscal policy fellow at the liberal-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

The GAO — Congress’s watchdog which deemed the pocket rescissions inconsistent with the law during Trump’s first term — concluded late last month the president lacked the legal authority to withhold the $800 million in funds beyond their expiration date.

The GAO is the only group that can sue the administration for violating the Impoundment Control Act under an August 2025 ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, but the office has not brought a lawsuit against the Trump administration.

Appropriations Chair Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) floated that Congress could authorize the GAO to sue — something it is already authorized to do — or outside groups can pursue their own lawsuits. She said she is considering adding guardrails against pocket rescissions in the next appropriations bills in December.

A spokesperson for Collins declined to comment further on her strategy to curtail pocket rescissions.

Golden contended that GAO wouldn’t have to sue the Trump administration if Congress passed his legislation, which goes beyond pocket rescissions. The Congressional Budget Reform Act would trigger automatic 14-day continuing resolutions to prevent a government shutdown. In addition, it would package Congress’s 12 annual appropriations bills into four minibuses, and require lawmakers to stay in session until they are completed.

The bill would also require a 60-vote threshold in the Senate to approve the president’s rescissions requests. In 2025, Congress voted along party lines to cancel $9.4 billion in rescissions proposed by the White House.

Trump’s more than $800 million in rescission requests includes $567 million for refugee and asylum-holder assistance programs administered by the Department of Health and Human Services. Other targets of the cuts include high school and college success programs for students in the U.S. and the Office of Minority Health.

Blue Dog Democrats told The Sun that Democrats should not adopt pocket rescissions and other budgetary maneuvers Trump has implemented should they come back to power.

Gluesenkamp Perez said Democrats who want to adopt Trump’s tactics fail both their colleagues in vulnerable seats and their constituents.

“We're seeing in this shift in the House, you'll lose your election, so you'll lose the chicken game in the short run. In the long term, you're fucking driving the economy into a ditch here,” said Gluesenkamp Perez, whose race is rated a toss-up by The Cook Political Report. “I'm hopeful that our colleagues are cognizant of the consequences of this for folks who are going to lose their seats.”

entries.title: U.S. Hits the International Criminal Court With Sweeping Sanctions
entries.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. "and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”
entries.content:
By Matthew Lee

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the U.S. believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts. Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

The sanctions block any assets the ICC as an institution might have in U.S. jurisdictions and set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.

Rubio said both Republicans and Democrats have deep reservations about the court, which was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might not otherwise be handled by the parties involved. But he said that only President Donald Trump was willing to move against the court.

“Both parties agree on this, but only President Trump has the resolve to take the action needed to end this threat once and for all," Rubio said. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens.

“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.”

ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.”

She also appealed to other ICC members for support. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law.”

Rubio added that the U.S. expects its allies to join in the actions against the ICC. Those include many NATO members in Europe and Japan.

“If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer," he said.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, posting on X, called the sanctions announcement “a deeply regrettable step. We stand firm in defence of the court.”

He said the six-month window before the sanctions take effect “creates scope for dialogue.”

As host state of the court, the Netherlands is a strong defender of the ICC.

___

Associated Press writers Mike Corder and Molly Quell in The Hague, Netherlands, contributed.

entries.title: Forecasted Hurricane Forces Trump to Change His Football Plans
entries.summary: The president was scheduled to attend Saturday’s Alabama-Georgia game, but Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall on the Gulf Coast.
entries.content:
With a hurricane bearing down on the Gulf Coast, President Donald Trump will not attend the Alabama-Georgia game in Tuscaloosa this weekend as previously planned.

Trump said in a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon that “it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!”

He added he hoped the “potentially unbelievable” game would go on, despite the weather, and he planned to visit both teams at a later date. Trump said he will instead travel to Tennessee for a campaign rally in an unnamed location.

Trump had been scheduled to travel to Bryant-Denny Stadium to watch Saturday night’s game, but Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall along Alabama’s coast and bring severe storms deeper into the state.

When asked Wednesday whether he still planned to travel to the game, Trump told reporters that he was unaware of the hurricane but indicated it could change his plans.

“If there’s a hurricane, I don’t want to do anything to take the focus of all of the great people that work on those things,” Trump said. “So we’ll have to see.”

The game would’ve been the second high-profile SEC game Trump had attended in the span of a few weeks. He took in the first half of the Tennessee-Texas game in Knoxville, Tennessee, on Sept. 26. And it would have been his second visit to Tuscaloosa to see Alabama play Georgia within the past two years. He attended in 2024 and remained for the entire game, which saw Alabama narrowly defeat the Bulldogs.

entries.title: Soldiers Are Already Looking for a Way Out of Hegseth’s Livestreamed Firing Squad
entries.summary: At least six soldiers are planning to file for preliminary religious exemptions, a nonprofit leader told The Sun. More are expected to follow.
entries.content:
Some soldiers are already panicking about the possibility of being asked or even forced to participate in the firing squad execution of Nidal Mikal Hasan, according to a religious freedom organization that advises U.S. military members.

Hasan, who killed 13 people during a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, in a spectacle that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said this week would be livestreamed publicly by the Trump administration.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it,” Hegseth told the conservative television network Real America’s Voice News on Thursday. “People need to understand there are serious consequences for these types of things.”

Just a day later, Michael L. Weinstein, the founder of the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, told The Washington Sun that he had spoken to six soldiers who are already looking to file for preliminary religious exemptions that would prevent them from being selected for the firing squad. He said that he anticipates between 120 and 180 service members to file accommodation requests in the coming weeks.

The MRFF is a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the religious freedom of service members and advocates for them when military policies or practices may infringe on their beliefs.

The service members expressed concerns about being part of what Weinstein called a “grotesque public spectacle” and fear that participating in the execution would violate the biblical commandment against murder. Two of the six service members are Catholic and four are Protestant.

“They feel they’re being used and manipulated,” Weinstein said. “Like chess pieces on a board.”

“Four have had preliminary indication that they are potentially vulnerable to be qualified to be on the firing squad,” Weinstein added, though he did not elaborate on what that indication was.

An execution order signed Monday by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directed Hasan be put to death by firing squad on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. Central Time. The order, issued after President Donald Trump approved Hasan’s death sentence on Oct. 2, designated the commandant of the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth as the execution officer.

The order cites Army Regulation 190-55, which governs military executions but does not specify how soldiers will be selected for the firing squad, whether their participation will be voluntary or how their identities will be protected. It also makes no mention of livestreaming the execution.

Soldiers ordered to participate in the execution would have little legal recourse to refuse, according to Steven Lepper, a retired Air Force major general and former deputy judge advocate general of the Air Force.

Although military regulations recognize conscientious objectors who oppose war in all its forms, they do not provide a comparable exemption for service members who object to a particular assignment, he said.

“This is one of those situations … that could be classified as lawful but awful,” Lepper said. “If a soldier is ordered to participate in a firing squad, there being no specific legal prohibitions against it, it would probably be considered a lawful order and one which the soldier has a duty to follow.”

Cynthia Smith, an Army spokesperson, could not provide further details about the selection of soldiers, the logistics of the broadcast or whether any legal objections had been filed.

None of the soldiers who spoke with the Military Religious Freedom Foundation claimed they’d actively been tapped to serve on the execution team.

As a precaution, however, Weinstein advised each of the soldiers to file the exemption requests, which would need to be reviewed by a chaplain and approved by a commanding general.

If their requests are denied, he’s advised them to file formal complaints against their commanders. Weinstein emphasized that being ordered to serve as part of a firing squad is consistent with laws governing military executions, but the public nature of a livestreamed event changes the stakes for participants.

He said one soldier told him: “I do not want my children or my family watching me pull a trigger.”

Several soldiers argued the public nature of the killing would violate a basic tenet of Christianity that prohibits sinning in pride.

It’s unclear how many soldiers would be a part of the execution team. South Carolina, which legalized firing squad executions in 2021, has used a crew of three shooters, all with live rounds, to kill death row inmates.

The Pentagon has not released details of the logistics and did not respond to a detailed series of questions or a request for comment from The Sun.

While lawful, Lepper warned that livestreaming Hasan’s execution could inflame extremists and turn him into a martyr. Lepper noted that the United States has long condemned public executions in other countries, raising questions about the precedent the Pentagon would set.

“Why would anyone want to inflame the passions of an enemy that we’re currently fighting?” he asked. “Why would we want to inflame the passions of the Muslim world by making Hassan a martyr?”

Weinstein agreed, saying, “This is his dream.”

”This will be viewed as an execution of Islam,” he said. “How could he possibly be martyred any better?”

Moreover, Weinstein said troops have questioned whether Hegseth is using the execution as a political ploy ahead of the midterms.

Weinstein said hundreds of soldiers have reached out to the Military Religious Freedom Foundation to share their concerns about the defense secretary’s acerbic leadership style and relentless focus on culture war issues.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have spoken out against Hegseth’s decision to livestream the execution — one of the rare issues where Republicans have spoken out against the Trump administration and publicly called for a reversal.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) excoriated the decision in an X post: “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

While speaking to reporters on Friday, Vice President JD Vance said he didn’t expect the livestream to actually take place — adding that even if it does, he plans not to watch.

“I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters Friday. “If it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not gonna be watching it.”
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: Calling for Satan? Wrong Number.
entries.summary: Capitol Hill Books sells books. Your lawmaker doesn’t work there, and neither does the Antichrist.
entries.content:
About once a day, someone calls Capitol Hill Books enraged. It's hard to make out exactly what they're mad about, but lately it's been about the U.S. Capitol being "the great den of Satan." They don't realize they're yelling at the wrong place.

"You've called a bookstore called Capitol Hill Books and not the actual Capitol," co-owner Kyle Burk responds. "I suggest you look for your particular congressperson that you're trying to reach."

The caller is usually still angry, especially now that they aren't getting what they want, which is to speak to someone with a big title about how they're ruining the country. They usually assert that they are exercising their First Amendment rights. One person specifically asked to speak with Satan.

"We assure them that we have no power other than to sell them used books,” said Burk, 50. “Once it goes to Satan, it’s an immediate hang up.”

The misdirected rage calls surge with the news, such as when Congress was debating the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. During discussions of the pandemic stimulus package, a caller demanded: "Put me through to AOC."

"It's kind of a classic, ‘Sir, this is a Wendy's’ meme scenario," Burk said. "We like our name. If this is the burden we have to live with, so be it."

With midterm elections less than a month away, Burk said the calls boil down to: “Is this Capitol Hill? Let me tell you why I’m angry. I don't like what you guys are doing up there. You're a bunch of crooks.”

None of the owners take it personally. They know the callers aren’t actually mad at a bookstore.

Earlier this week, the store posted on Instagram: “Friendly reminder that we are Capitol Hill Books, a bookstore, not 'the' Capitol Hill, the seat of satanic power you keep calling to yell at us about. We wish, obviously, but sadly no.”

The store doesn’t avoid political discussions, which often reflect just how liberal residents are in this city. Customers have tacked fliers on the wall: an immigration film festival, an Amnesty International report on Sudan, a petition to oppose plans for a new Immigration and Customs Enforcement headquarters in D.C.

Capitol Hill Books is packed into a row house across from Eastern Market. There are 20,000 books, jammed anywhere the owners could find space. On the second floor, there's a section on dirigibles, right next to erotica, but you need a ladder to reach it. A couple years ago, Burk said, they moved the law books into the bathroom.

The store doesn't have voicemail set up, Burk said, because "That would be chaos."
entries.author: Ellie Silverman

entries.title: Trump Says He Struck a Diesel Deal With Putin to Lower Fuel Prices
entries.summary: The president said the deal would lead to diesel prices “COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to boost global diesel supplies, seeking to bring down soaring fuel prices just weeks before the midterm elections.

In a Truth Social post, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace,” followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward.

Russia would then deliver an additional 3 million tons within a short period, depending on the condition of its refineries, Trump said.

Trump predicted that the Russian supplies, along with U.S. control of the Strait of Hormuz, would send diesel prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"

He did not say whether he offered Putin anything in return.

Shortly after the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to reach global markets, including into the U.S. through April.

The White House referred to the Treasury Department’s announcement of the temporary license. The State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The agreement comes as Trump faces pressure to bring down fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Diesel prices have risen roughly 70% since the U.S. war with Iran began in February, reaching a national average of about $6.28 per gallon Friday, according to AAA.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply criticized the agreement, warning that easing sanctions would help Russia prolong its war against Ukraine.

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy."

Trump signed legislation last month expanding sanctions on Russia, including its energy industry and financial institutions, over the war in Ukraine.

The U.S. has prohibited imports of Russian oil and petroleum products, including diesel, since 2022.

Russia has also restricted diesel exports through the end of October to protect its domestic market after Ukrainian attacks damaged refineries.

Putin said earlier this month that Russia would not resume diesel exports to global markets until sanctions were lifted, Reuters reported.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Hegseth Says an Execution Will Be Streamed. Vance Isn’t So Sure.
entries.summary: And if there is a stream? The vice president says he’s “not going to be watching it."
entries.content:
Despite Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of a convicted terrorist would be livestreamed, Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the public display will happen. If it does, he says he won’t be among those watching.

“I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters traveling with him in Ohio. “Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people. Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it."

Nidal Malik Hasan, an ex-U.S. Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood in 2009. He was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013. Vance called the shooting the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11.

The Defense Department announced Monday that Hasan would face a firing squad. But Hegseth’s plan to stream the execution online faces a growing list of Republicans publicly opposing the idea, including a member of the House Armed Services Committee that oversees the Pentagon.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said on Thursday that the decision was “beyond disgusting.”

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do,” Tillis posted on X. “It should not be happening in America.”

That sentiment was echoed on Friday by Rep. Austin Scott (R-Georgia), a member of the House Armed Services committee, who posted that “livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”

President Donald Trump approved an execution by firing squad. Trump talked about the execution during a Columbus Day event on Friday but didn’t mention it being livestreamed.

The White House referred questions about how and where the execution would be streamed to the Pentagon. The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment on the plan or on Vance’s comments.

Trump’s seal of approval hasn’t kept opposition to the online execution from growing within his party.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) urged Hegseth to reconsider broadcasting it, citing the Roman philosopher Seneca’s belief that “Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them.”

Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania), who’s in danger of losing his seat in November, said that Hegseth shouldn’t use an execution as entertainment.

“The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment,” Bresnahan posted on X. “Their pain deserves respect, not a public show.”
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Judge Bars the Deportation of a Man Shot By an ICE Agent in NYC
entries.summary: The court also ordered immigration agents not to move Oscar Bergal outside of New York or New Jersey.
entries.content:
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from deporting a Dominican man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Thursday in New York City.

U.S. District Judge J. Paul Oetken also ordered ICE not to move Oscar Bergal, 28, whom law enforcement initially identified as Belgal, out of New York and New Jersey. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during a press conference Friday morning that Bergal had been taken out of New York.

In the same petition for Bergal in federal court seeking a temporary restraining order, U.S. District Judge John Cronan ordered an in-person hearing Friday afternoon. He told the government to be prepared to discuss Bergal’s current location, his location when the petition was filed and other circumstances.

An ICE agent shot seven times at a car with Bergal and his 5-year-old child inside, striking the man in the neck, Jessica Tisch, New York Police Department’s commissioner, said during a press conference Thursday night.

The shooting took place around 4 p.m. in Marble Hill, a northern Manhattan neighborhood. Two NYPD officers took Bergal to the hospital in a police car, according to body camera footage the department released Friday morning.

Attorneys from immigrant rights’ advocacy group Make the Road New York filed a petition in court seeking Bergal’s release.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Thursday he had spent two hours trying to negotiate Bergal’s release.

“Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani said. “Just moments ago, ICE put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away."
entries.author: Jackie Llanos

entries.title: Trump’s Catering-Truck Escape From AF1 Wasn’t the First: Secret Service Chief
entries.summary: Sean Curran told CBS News he wished that operation had never been publicly reported.
entries.content:
Secret Service Director Sean Curran said in an interview that the agency had used subterfuge and decoy planes to conceal President Donald Trump’s whereabouts before the secret operation that allowed him to leave Turkey this summer amid reported Iranian threats.

“Look, that’s not the first time we’ve done that,” Curran told CBS News’ Norah O’Donnell in a preview for a “60 Minutes” segment scheduled to air Sunday.

Curran also said he wished the operation had never been made public.

“We wish that wasn't reported because that takes some of our tactics away from being able to do something similar again,” he told O'Donnell.

The maneuver took place July 8, when Trump was leaving a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, amid intelligence about a possible Iranian missile attack targeting his plane.

Trump initially boarded Air Force One in view of cameras before secretly leaving the aircraft through an airport catering truck and transferring to a smaller military plane.

Air Force One then flew to Britain with journalists, White House staff and senior administration officials aboard, while Trump traveled separately. Many passengers were unaware the president was no longer on the plane.

Trump later confirmed the switch, saying the Secret Service and military wanted him aboard a different aircraft because of the threat.

The tactic has been used by previous presidents. In March 2000, President Bill Clinton traveled to Pakistan aboard an unmarked aircraft while another plane resembling Air Force One served as a decoy.

Unlike Trump’s flight, however, the Clinton White House briefed a representative of the traveling press corps about the security arrangements.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Trump Names an Adviser to Trump Media as White House Press Secretary
entries.summary: Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia also briefly worked as a spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump named conservative commentator Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary on Friday, filling a role that has sat vacant for more than a month since Karoline Leavitt’s departure.

In a Truth Social post announcing his pick, Trump credited Zacharia’s appearances on Fox News and Newsmax and her work in swing states during his 2024 campaign for landing her the gig. He called her “a devoted fan and member of MAGA” with “an unblemished record of support.” He also again praised Leavitt, whom he called “fabulous.”

Zacharia briefly served as a spokesperson and deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security for about six weeks in early 2026. Most recently, she works as a communications adviser at Trump Media and Technology Group, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Zacharia wrote in a February social media post that she was “proud to serve” Trump and then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem in her new DHS role.

During a recent segment on Fox News’ “Jesse Watters Primetime,” Zacharia said she had signed all four of her children up for Trump Accounts, the federal investment accounts for minors Trump again touted this week.

Trump has posted clips of an August Fox News segment featuring Zacharia on Truth Social several times. In one, she says Trump is “not getting enough praise” for a decline in fentanyl deaths and calls him the most effective president “for the border and interior enforcement.”

After her stint at DHS, Zacharia served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative advocacy group founded by Richard Grenell, Trump’s presidential envoy for special missions.

The White House chose not to replace Leavitt as she took maternity leave for a few months earlier this year, and it also never named anyone as an interim press secretary after Leavitt departed permanently at the end of August. Instead, a rotating band of Cabinet secretaries, Trump officials — and even Vice President JD Vance — took turns briefing reporters in recent months.
entries.author: Ayah Ali-Ahmad

entries.title: D.C. Elections Board Asks National Guard to Stay Away From Ballot Drop Boxes
entries.summary: Guard members were seen standing next to a drop box in Foggy Bottom this week.
entries.content:
Reports of National Guard troops standing next to a D.C. ballot drop box in Foggy Bottom on Thursday have prompted complaints from some residents and an official request from the D.C. Board of Elections that it not happen again.

“We are addressing the concerns with the National Guard directly and have requested that they impose limitations on the placement of National Guard service members near drop boxes and other voting locations in the District,” said board spokesperson Sarah Graham.

The ballot drop box wasn’t in use when the National Guard troops were filmed standing next to it.

“We are aware of imagery circulating online of service members standing near a ballot drop box. Maintaining public trust is a top priority, and JTF-DC service members are directed not to monitor or secure polling locations,” said a spokesperson for the Joint Task Force, which is in charge of the D.C. deployment, in response to questions from The Washington Sun.

“JTF-DC is actively addressing this specific instance and remains fully committed to conducting its missions professionally, lawfully, and with respect for the public's constitutional rights,” the spokesperson said.

The city’s 55 drop boxes opened Friday morning and will be available for voters to drop off their ballots through the end of Election Day, which is Nov. 3.

Ballot drop boxes are popular with voters; for the June primary, more than 63,000 voters used them to return their ballots, representing roughly 40% of all votes cast. The boxes tend to be in high-traffic areas — including by Metro stations like in Foggy Bottom.

It is against federal law for troops to be deployed around polling places.

Reactions to the video that circulated on social media at least partly reflect the ongoing discomfort that some D.C. residents still feel with having the National Guard deployed in D.C. on President Donald Trump’s orders. While he has credited their presence with helping drive down crime, critics say their deployment is unnecessary and sets a troubling precedent around the use of the military for law enforcement.

As of Thursday, 2,864 National Guard troops were deployed in D.C., down from a high of more than 5,000 during the summer months. Roughly 2,300 of them are from 18 states outside of D.C., with Georgia, Mississippi and Florida having the biggest contingents.

There have been recent complaints about Guard members operating around D.C. schools, and city officials have asked that they refrain from doing so. Ward 2 D.C. Council member Brooke Pinto will hold a public hearing on Oct. 14 to hear from residents on their experiences with the National Guard in D.C.

Some of the concerns with the Guard members at the D.C. ballot box could also stem from broader worries about the Trump administration’s reported plans to deploy federal agents around polling places for the November election. This month, the Department of Homeland Security said it has no plans to station ICE agents at the polls.

The Trump administration also attempted to rein in mail voting generally this year; D.C. joins a handful of states that automatically send all registered voters a mail ballot, and most voters now prefer that to voting in person. Those efforts were stymied by litigation.

Still, changes to how the U.S. Postal Service postmarks ballots have prompted election officials to warn voters that if they’re going to use USPS to mail in their ballot, they should ensure that the postmark is not dated after Election Day, which would lead to the ballot being rejected.

A weeklong period of in-person early voting in D.C. kicks off Oct. 26.
entries.author: Martin Austermuhle

entries.title: The U.S. Has Kept Its Distance From the Saudi-Houthi Fight, But Can That Last?
entries.summary: With the conflict escalating, experts and officials worry the Trump administration could be forced to play a more central role in the fighting.
entries.content:
As the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen escalates, the Trump administration is resisting requests to enter the fighting directly, even as Washington provides military assistance to the Saudis. But mounting Houthi attacks, doubts about the Saudi strategy and the conflict’s ties to the Iran war are driving questions from officials and experts about how long the U.S. can keep its distance.

The Trump administration is already providing the Saudis with intelligence and aerial refueling, a U.S. official told The Washington Sun, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter. The official said American involvement includes “advising the Saudis to remove questionable targets from their strike lists” because of concerns about civilian casualties.

More than 100 American military personnel are advising Saudi Arabia on its bombing runs in Yemen. President Donald Trump also wants to sell the Saudis thousands of American-made precision-guided bombs and 48 F-35 fighter jets — plans opposed by congressional Democrats. With weapons and training from Iran, the Houthis have struck Saudi airports and oil infrastructure that is crucial to global energy flows, which are already strained by the Iran war.

Trump has reportedly dodged requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct military support. People familiar with administration thinking told The Sun the White House is resistant to deeper entanglement for now.

“We can avoid it for the time being,” said one person familiar with Trump administration officials’ thinking who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. The person emphasized Trump’s dissatisfaction with Operation Rough Rider, the 2025 American campaign against the Houthis that failed to significantly weaken the group despite its $1 billion price tag.

Some U.S. officials doubt the Saudi approach, noting that the country pushed the United Arab Emirates — another U.S. partner in the region — out of Yemen earlier this year. The UAE was, like the Saudis, supporting anti-Houthi fighters on the ground.

“I have discerned no appetite whatsoever to expand [U.S. involvement] to bail out the Saudis,” the person familiar said.

Annelle Sheline, a researcher at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told The Sun she was unsurprised by U.S. frustration with Saudi choices. Still, Sheline said that the Saudis viewed UAE-linked Yemeni separatists as an emerging security concern in a similar way to the Houthis.

The conflict’s recent escalation may have presented an opportunity for Saudi Arabia to rally more international support as it takes on the Houthis because of global concern about the Yemeni group’s role in helping Iran disrupt oil and gas shipments. France is shielding Saudi energy infrastructure, and Britain is also refueling Saudi jets, while Pakistan and Turkey have deployed troops to Saudi Arabia.

Trump may prove unwilling to join the coalition until after America’s midterm elections, as the unpopular Iran war continues to be a problem politically for Republicans.

“My expectation would be that at some point, maybe he does announce post-midterms he’s fine with doing a couple of very specific, very targeted bombing campaigns alongside the Saudis,” said Elizabeth Dent, a former Pentagon official who worked on Gulf security during the Biden administration. “The inclination is to be as supportive as possible without taking the lead.”

The Saudis’ contributions to Trump’s family businesses, including a $2 billion investment in a fund run by his son-in-law Jared Kushner, could also bolster their expectation that they are owed U.S. support.

“I imagine all MBS has to do is say, ‘Trump, I personally enriched you!’” Sheline said.

The person close to the administration told The Sun they expect the Saudis to keep emphasizing their ties to Trump as they seek help, but they’ve had “no luck thus far.”

A resumed U.S. offensive against Iran could also push the administration to target the Houthis, if the Yemeni group launches further strikes in solidarity with Tehran. The Pentagon has already prepared fresh Iran war plans, according to The New York Times, and American military forces remain concentrated in the region.

Still, some are urging caution about the prospect of another U.S. campaign in Yemen, after attacks under presidents Trump, Joe Biden, Barack Obama and George W. Bush failed to stem security threats out of the country and drove humanitarian crises.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who visited Riyadh this week, told reporters he believes the Saudis want to push the Houthis out of more Yemeni territory but would eventually settle on a truce with the group. Meanwhile, the senator argued the U.S. is already embroiled in the fighting, pointing to the military advisers and refueling operations.

“To me, that’s war,” Murphy said. He added Congress may try to stop Trump from continuing American involvement.

Sen. Ed Markey (D-Massachusetts) is already leading an effort to block 10,000 additional American bombs for Saudi Arabia. In an Oct. 5 letter to senators, more than 30 antiwar and human rights groups pushed senators to support Markey’s resolution, arguing that it is consistent for legislators who have voted to restrict Trump’s Iran war to oppose moves that could deepen the conflict in Yemen.

Observers note the potential heavy toll of the fighting and a feedback loop of violence if a deal is the endgame.

A regional diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the thinking among officials, told The Sun that Saudi anxiety about the Houthis is “understandable” but added: “Military pressure tends to harden positions rather than bring parties to the table.”

Oman, another U.S. regional partner, has maintained channels to Riyadh and the Houthis. The diplomat said the country is expected to soon begin mediation between the two.
entries.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed, Joe Gould

entries.title: Trump-Aligned Super PAC Ran an Ad Attacking a Native American Candidate — Featuring the Wrong Person
entries.summary: No Going Back PAC has since corrected the ad.
entries.content:
No Going Back PAC, a Trump-aligned super PAC, ran an ad attacking Jonathan Nez, a Native American candidate in a competitive Arizona House district. But it twice showed images of another Native American politician instead.

The 30-second spot erroneously showed photos of Myron Lizer, who held tribal office alongside Nez. Nez is the former president of the Navajo Nation and is now the Democratic nominee for Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, which is represented by his Republican opponent, Rep. Eli Crane.

The ad, which began airing on Friday and is set to run through Tuesday, twice featured photos of Lizer, who was Nez’s Republican vice president during his time as president of the Navajo Nation.

“Eli Crane and his billionaire backers are so scared of an Indigenous sheepherder from Shonto, Arizona, they rushed a $700k ad against me. But they care so little about the voters of AZ-02 they couldn’t get it right,” Nez told The Washington Sun in a statement. “The voters of AZ-02 are tired of their broken promises and disregard for the real challenges they are facing. I guess they don’t care to know my face, but on November 3rd they’ll hear my voice.”

The No Going Back PAC is planning to spend more than $650,000 on the advertisement, according to AdImpact.

“The ad was corrected shortly after it aired,” a spokesperson for the super PAC told The Sun in a statement.

AdImpact now shows an updated version of the advertisement with the correct photos showing Nez.

The ad goes after Nez on affordability and accusations of fraud.

Lizer did not respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Democrats Hope They Can Ride a ‘Perfect Storm’ in Texas
entries.summary: State Rep. James Talarico has been attacked for not campaigning as Democrats pin their hopes on his promising campaign.
entries.content:
In one of the most high-profile Senate races in the country, the leading candidate has been noticeably absent.

Texas Republicans for days attacked state Rep. James Talarico for leaving the campaign trail for nine days, which Talarico’s team said was because he was recovering from the flu.

On Friday, videos of Talarico walking and shaking hands with people appeared on social media. His campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told The Washington Sun in a statement that “James Talarico is back on the campaign trail talking to voters at Austin City Limits.”

Talarico is expected to do additional campaigning this weekend, as well as appear on a CNN town hall Oct. 14.

Despite the absence from the trail, Talarico appears to be giving Democrats their best shot in a generation to win a statewide race in Texas — something they haven't done since 1994. Less than four weeks out from Election Day, Democrats are bullish about flipping the seat, buoyed by national attention, polling that shows Talarico leading state Attorney General Ken Paxton by roughly 5 percentage points, and Talarico's staggering most-recent fundraising numbers: $31.6 million to Paxton's $18 million.

If Texas were to elect a Democratic senator, it would help Democrats win back the majority in the Senate and change the fabric of the 2028 presidential election.

“We've got a cartoonishly corrupt Republican nominee in Ken Paxton, we've got a historically unpopular president in Donald Trump, and we've got a great communicator and fundraiser in James Talarico,” said Luke Warford, founding partner of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund, a group in Texas aimed at building Democratic infrastructure. “Those three things add up to mean that Democrats might actually win Texas for the first time in a generation this year.”

One Democratic operative working on Senate races called the situation for the Senate election in Texas unique for this cycle, saying the stars might align for Democrats to flip the seat.

“It's truly a perfect storm of conditions. You have one of the worst Republican candidates in the country, the most unpopular Republican Senate candidate in Texas history,” the operative said. “James Talarico is an extraordinary candidate. He is very compelling on the stump. He's a great fundraiser. He speaks to people in a language that sounds familiar to them, on a religious level and because he’s a very bipartisan guy.”

Paxton’s being hit with a drip-drip-drip of leaked audio published in different publications revealing his criticism of Trump’s administration, as well as blaming the Republican D.C. establishment for issues in his Senate campaign.

His issues run back before the leaked meeting. In 2023, he was impeached on more than a dozen articles, including bribery, unfitness for office and obstruction of justice, and was acquitted by the state Senate in a high-profile trial. Since then, he’s faced a messy public divorce from state Sen. Angela Paxton, though she has urged voters to cast their ballots for the Republican ticket.

“[What is happening with Paxton] is a fucking total disaster,” a Republican strategist told The Washington Sun. “Talarico will likely be there for six years. He'll be a national star. He's going to help build the Democratic Party. He's going to recruit candidates. He's going to build the most massive donor file a Democrat in Texas has ever had. It is a disaster from 19 different angles.”

Paxton’s had immense help from outside fundraising groups, but there’s still concern from Republicans it won’t be enough to help him win. One sign of how much trouble he could be in may be the repeated trips to the state from his most prominent surrogate, President Donald Trump. Earlier this week the president took his third trip to Texas this cycle, and Vice President JD Vance is expected to go on Tuesday.

“I wouldn't say we're concerned [about winning],” said a Republican aide close to the Paxton campaign. “In the last two and a half weeks or so, where the cavalry has kind of arrived for him, I think you're starting to see that movement, and we feel that [Paxton is] in a pretty good spot to kind of bring those undecideds that are, you know, leaning Republicans back home to him and push him over the top.”

The last time the state had such a tight race was October 2018. Texas' U.S. Senate race had the nation's attention for a midterm year in President Donald Trump’s first term. Polls showed Sen. Ted Cruz leading then-Rep. Beto O'Rourke by mid-to-high single digits, but on Election Day the Republican incumbent won by just 2.6 percentage points, the closest Texas Senate race in decades. (Cruz beat Rep. Colin Allred in a presidential election year by 9 percentage points.)

For years, Democrats have pointed to those results as proof the state was within reach.

The race is on track to become the most expensive Senate contest in history, a sign of how competitive both parties expect it to be in the final stretch. According to the media tracking firm AdImpact, ad spending in the general election has reached $255 million as of Friday, making it one of the most expensive Senate races in history.
entries.author: Daniella Diaz

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Firing Squad
entries.content:
THE LATEST

JD Vance told reporters he’s “not going to be watching” any livestreamed execution of the Fort Hood shooter — and cast doubt on whether the government will actually broadcast it.

  • “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” he said. “Let’s sort of, see — I think it’s going to happen in December, when he’s executed.”
Scoop: Religious freedom groups say soldiers are preemptively attempting to opt out of participating in the firing squad, with one telling an advocate: “I do not want my children or my family watching me pull a trigger.”

Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia has been offered the position of White House press secretary, Donald Trump announced today.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Federal immigration agents who shot a man with his 5-year-old son in the car were wearing body cameras that were turned on, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said today.

  • A federal judge blocked the administration from deporting the man, who is from the Dominican Republic.
Trump announced he has reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to boost global diesel supplies, seeking to bring down soaring fuel prices.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said the agency used subterfuge and decoy planes to conceal Trump’s whereabouts before the secret operation that allowed him to leave Turkey this summer amid reported Iranian threats.

Trump’s latest effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook includes establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements on mortgage applications.

As the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen escalates, the Trump administration is resisting requests to enter the fighting directly, even as Washington provides military assistance to the Saudis.

The FBI wants to hire the UFC to train its special agents under a one-year deal that would bypass the competitive bidding process typically used for federal contracts.





THE HILL

Exclusive: Moderate Democrats are introducing a bill to end pocket rescissions and wrest back congressional control over government spending from the president.
